source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Preparing to Ride
source.sourceQuote: Tinted eye protection should not be worn when little outside light is available.

rules.text: Boots or shoes should be high and sturdy enough to cover your ankles and give them support.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Preparing to Ride
source.sourceQuote: Boots or shoes should be high and sturdy enough to cover your ankles and give them support.

lessons.plainEnglish:
Gear is 'right' when it protects you, and the manual names three things: a DOT-compliant helmet, face or eye protection, and protective clothing. The helmet case is made with numbers, not opinion. One crash in five produces head or neck injuries. Helmeted riders are three times more likely to survive a head injury. And the common excuses do not survive contact with the research: a DOT-compliant helmet still lets you see as far to the sides as necessary, and most crashes happen on short trips under five miles, a few minutes after starting out — exactly the ride people skip the helmet for.

Eye protection is a separate requirement, not part of the helmet question. A plastic impact-resistant faceshield protects your whole face. Goggles protect your eyes but not the rest of your face. A windshield on the motorcycle is not a substitute for either, and neither are eyeglasses or sunglasses, which can blow off when you turn your head. Tinted protection has its own limit: do not wear it when little outside light is available.

Clothing is the layer people treat as optional and shouldn't. Jacket and pants should cover arms and legs completely and fit snugly enough not to flap. Leather offers the most protection; sturdy synthetics offer a lot. Boots should cover and support the ankles with hard, slip-resistant soles and short heels. Gloves should be leather or similar durable material. Hearing protection reduces noise while still letting you hear car horns or sirens.
lessons.whyItMatters:
Every other topic in this manual is about avoiding the crash. This one is about what happens if you do not. It is the only topic where the right answer costs you nothing at the moment of the crash because the decision was already made in the driveway.

The exam tests the specific comparisons: faceshield versus goggles versus windshield, and when tinted protection is wrong. Those are one-sentence rules with a clear ranking, and they are easy marks once you have the ranking straight.
lessons.example: You are riding to a shop two miles away on a warm evening and think about leaving the helmet behind. The manual's own numbers argue against it: most crashes happen on short trips of less than five miles, just a few minutes after starting out, and one crash in five produces head or neck injuries. You put the helmet on and fasten it, because an unfastened helmet can come off before it gets a chance to protect you. As the light drops you also swap the tinted shield for a clear one, because tinted eye protection should not be worn when little outside light is available.

lessons.plainEnglish:
A motorcycle that does not fit you is harder to control at exactly the moments control matters. The manual's fit test is simple: your feet should reach the ground while you are seated, and the controls should be easy to operate. Smaller motorcycles are usually easier for beginners. At a minimum, a street-legal motorcycle needs a headlight, taillight and brake light, front and rear brakes, turn signals, a horn, and two mirrors.

Unfamiliarity is its own hazard. More than half of all crashes involve riders with less than five months of experience on that motorcycle. If you borrow a bike, get familiar with it away from traffic first — find the turn signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel valve and engine cut-off switch and operate them without looking. If you lend yours, make sure the borrower is licensed and knows how to ride.

A motorcycle needs more frequent attention than a car, because the same minor failure that inconveniences a driver can put a rider down. The pre-ride inspection takes a few minutes and belongs before every ride. T-CLOCS is the memory aid: Tires and wheels, Controls, Lights and electrics, Oil and other fluids, Chassis, Stands. Among the specifics worth remembering: each brake alone should hold the motorcycle, the throttle should snap back to fully closed when released, mirrors are adjusted before starting so you can see the lane behind and the lane next to you, and the side stand's spring should hold it tightly up.
lessons.whyItMatters:
Mechanical problems on a motorcycle turn into control problems immediately. A throttle that does not snap closed, a soft brake, a stand that drops — each is a minute's check before the ride and a crash during it.

The borrowing statistic is also a question the exam likes, because riders assume crashes are about speed or skill level in general. They are strongly about familiarity with this particular machine.
lessons.example: A friend lends you their bike for the weekend. Before touching a public road you sit on it and check that your feet reach the ground and the controls fall to hand. You run T-CLOCS: tire pressure and tread, each brake alone holding the bike, the throttle snapping shut when you let go, both headlight beams and all four turn signals, oil and brake fluid levels, the chain's adjustment, and the side stand springing firmly up. You adjust the mirrors while stopped so each shows the lane behind and the lane beside you, then ride the first few miles away from traffic.

rules.text: Blame doesn't matter when someone is injured in a crash.

source.chapterTitle: Preparing to Ride
source.sourceQuote: Blame doesn't matter when someone is injured in a crash.

lessons.plainEnglish:
The manual rejects the word 'accident' for what happens in traffic. An accident is an unforeseen event that occurs without fault or negligence; most people involved in a crash should probably claim some responsibility for what took place. Its example is deliberately even-handed: a driver runs a yellow turning red, and you pull into the intersection on green without checking. It was the driver's responsibility to stop. It was equally your responsibility to look before moving out.

From that follows the operating assumption for every other topic: as a rider you cannot be sure that other operators will see you or yield the right of way. So the manual lists what actually lessens your chances of a crash — be visible with proper clothing, headlight and lane position; communicate your intentions with signals, brake light and lane position; maintain an adequate space cushion when following, being followed, lane sharing, passing and being passed; search your path of travel 12 seconds ahead; identify and separate hazards; and be prepared to act with skills like firm braking or swerving.

The closing line is the point of the whole section: blame does not matter when someone is injured in a crash.
lessons.whyItMatters:
Being in the right is not protection. A rider who is legally blameless and physically injured has still lost. Every strategy later in the manual — lane position, SEE, covering the controls, conspicuity — is an application of this one idea.

The 12-second search distance is also a specific, testable number, and it pairs with the 2-second and 4-second figures in the SEE topic. Learn all three together.
lessons.example: Your light turns green at a busy intersection. Someone on the cross street is still moving as their light goes red. If you treat green as permission and roll, the crash is available to both of you. Instead you search the intersection before moving, keep your headlight on and your lane position where oncoming drivers can see you, and cover the clutch and brakes. You were entitled to go; you looked first anyway, because blame is no use to an injured rider.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: ROLL - Roll on the throttle to maintain or slightly increase speed.

lessons.plainEnglish:
Control starts with how you sit. Arms slightly bent so you can press on the handlebars without reaching, hands even with or below your elbows, right wrist flat so you cannot accidentally roll on too much throttle. Knees against the tank for balance in turns, feet firmly on the footrests with toes up — pointed-down toes can catch between the road and the footrest.

Braking is where riders lose the most. Always use both brakes every time you slow or stop, so the habit is there in an emergency. The front brake is the powerful one: it can provide 70% or more of your total stopping power, and it is safe to use if you use it properly. Squeeze it smoothly, firmly and with progressively more force rather than grabbing, because as weight transfers forward more traction becomes available at the front and you can then brake harder. At the rear, apply light-to-lighter pressure, because weight leaving the rear takes rear traction with it. Maximum straight-line braking is both brakes fully applied without locking either wheel.

Lean angle changes all of that. Any time the motorcycle is leaned over, the traction available for braking is reduced, and the greater the lean angle the more likely the tires are to lose grip. To stop quickly in a curve, get the motorcycle as perpendicular to the road as you can and then brake; if conditions do not allow, brake smoothly and gradually, reducing lean as you slow and increasing brake pressure as traction returns.

Turns have four steps that overlap in practice: SLOW, LOOK, PRESS, ROLL. Reduce speed before the turn. Look through the turn to where you want to go, turning just your head, not your shoulders, eyes level with the horizon. Press the handgrip on the side you want to go — press left, lean left, go left. Roll on the throttle to maintain or slightly increase speed, which stabilises the motorcycle. In ordinary turns the rider and motorcycle lean together; in slow, tight turns you counterbalance, leaning the motorcycle only and keeping your body upright.
lessons.whyItMatters:
Improper braking remains a significant contributing factor in many motorcycle crashes, and the single most common pattern is under-using the front brake and over-using the rear. Learning where the stopping power actually is — 70% or more at the front — is what turns an emergency stop from a skid into a stop.

The turn steps are equally practical. Riders who brake in the middle of a corner rather than before it, or who look at the hazard instead of through the turn to the exit, are the ones who run wide. Both errors are fixed by the same four-word sequence.
lessons.example: You are approaching a tightening right-hand bend a little faster than you would like. Before the bend you close the throttle and apply both brakes — SLOW, while you are still upright and have full braking traction. You turn just your head and look through the corner to where you want to be — LOOK. You press the right handgrip, the motorcycle leans right and goes right — PRESS. Through the corner you roll on the throttle slightly, which settles the suspension — ROLL. If you had left the braking until you were leaned over, the traction available for braking would already have been reduced, and hard braking there is how riders skid.

rules.text: One absolute, however, is to avoid riding in another vehicle's blind spot.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Keeping Your Distance
source.sourceQuote: One absolute, however, is to avoid riding in another vehicle's blind spot.

lessons.plainEnglish:
A cushion of space is what converts someone else's mistake into a near miss instead of a crash: more time to respond, more space to manoeuvre, and an escape path. Each traffic lane gives a motorcycle three paths of travel, and your lane choice should increase your ability to see and be seen, keep you out of blind spots, avoid surface hazards, communicate intentions, avoid windblast, provide an escape path, and set up for turns. Ride in path 2 or 3 when problems are on your left only, path 1 or 2 when hazards are on your right only, and path 2 — the centre — when vehicles are on both sides. No portion of the lane needs to be avoided as a rule, including the centre; just remember the centre third is where debris and oil drippings collect, and avoid big buildups of oil and grease at busy intersections and tollbooths.

Following distance is time, not car lengths. In traffic, motorcycles need as much distance to stop as cars, so the normal minimum is two seconds. Gauge it by picking a marker and counting 'one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two' as the vehicle ahead passes it; reaching the marker before 'two' means you are too close. Open it to three seconds or more if the pavement is slippery, if you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, or if traffic is heavy enough that someone may squeeze in.

Behind you is the other half. Speeding up to lose a tailgater only produces a tailgater at higher speed. The better answer is to get them in front of you: let them pass, or slow down and open up extra space ahead so there is room for both of you to stop. When you are being passed, stay in the centre portion of your lane — away from extended mirrors, objects thrown from windows, and blasts of wind from larger vehicles. Cars and motorcycles need a full lane, and lane sharing is usually prohibited; keep a centre-portion position wherever a driver might be tempted to squeeze past.
lessons.whyItMatters:
Following distance is one of the few things on the road that is entirely inside your control and instantly adjustable. 'Following too closely' is a frequent factor in crashes involving motorcyclists, and the fix costs nothing but a slightly later arrival.

The exam tests the numbers — two seconds normally, three or more when conditions are poor — and it tests the tailgater answer, where the intuitive response (speed up) is the wrong one.
lessons.example: A pickup truck sits a metre off your rear wheel on a wet road. Speeding up would just move the problem to a higher speed. Instead you move to a lane position that invites the pass and let them by; when they will not pass, you slow gently and open extra space ahead, so there is room for both of you to stop if the traffic in front brakes. The wet surface has also raised your own following distance from two seconds to three or more, and once the truck has gone past you return to the centre portion of the lane.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - SEE
source.sourceQuote: Apply the old adage “one step at a time” to handle two or more hazards.

lessons.plainEnglish:
SEE is Search, Evaluate, Execute — the framework that turns looking out of the windscreen into a decision. Search is active, not passive: scan the environment ahead, to the sides and behind to catch hazards before they arise, and focus on finding potential escape paths, especially around intersections, shopping areas, and school and construction zones. The manual gives three lead times to structure the search. At least 2 seconds is your following distance. Anything within 4 seconds of your path is immediate, because 4 seconds is roughly enough time and space to swerve or brake for a fixed hazard or for something entering your path. And you look further out still, to an area it would take about 12 seconds to reach, which is what gives you time to prepare before a situation becomes urgent.

Evaluate means thinking about how hazards can interact to create risks for you. Road and surface characteristics — potholes, guardrails, bridges, poles, trees — shape your strategy. Traffic control devices tell you what is about to happen. Vehicles and other traffic may move into your path. Escape paths need to be available, in front or to the sides.

Execute is the action, carried out with smoothness and precision. You have three tools: communicate your presence with lights and/or horn; adjust your speed by accelerating, stopping or slowing; and adjust your position or direction by swerving, changing lanes, or moving within your lane. When two or more hazards appear at once, apply 'one step at a time' — adjust speed to permit the hazards to separate, then deal with them one at a time as single hazards. With three or more, evaluate the consequences of each and give equal distance to the hazards. In high-risk areas, cover the clutch and both brakes to reduce the time you need to react.
lessons.whyItMatters:
Almost every specific rule later in the manual — lane position at intersections, covering the controls, following distance, swerving — is SEE applied to one situation. Learning the framework means you can reason your way to an answer on an exam question about a situation the manual never spells out.

The three lead times are also pure exam material. They are easy to confuse with each other: 2 seconds is the gap behind the vehicle ahead, 4 seconds is the immediate danger zone, 12 seconds is the long search.
lessons.example: You are approaching a shopping-centre entrance. Search: a car is waiting to turn out of the entrance, a delivery van is parked blocking part of your view, and a pedestrian is stepping off the kerb further on. Evaluate: the parked van hides the car's view of you and yours of anything beyond it, and the car and the pedestrian could both need your road within the same two seconds. Execute, one step at a time: you ease off to let the two hazards separate, cover the clutch and both brakes, move to the lane position that puts you in the waiting driver's field of view, and deal with the car first and the pedestrian second.

lessons.plainEnglish:
The greatest potential for conflict between you and other traffic is at intersections, and an intersection is not only a crossroads — it can be a driveway on a residential street, or anywhere traffic may cross your path of travel. Over one-half of motorcycle/car crashes are caused by drivers violating a rider's right-of-way. The specific dangers the manual names are cars that turn left in front of you, including cars turning left from the lane on your right, and cars on side streets that pull into your lane.

The manual then removes the comfort most riders reach for: there are no guarantees that others see you, and you should never count on eye contact, because too often a driver looks right at a motorcyclist and still fails to see him or her. The only eyes you can count on are your own. If a car can enter your path, assume that it will.

The strategy is concrete. Ride with your headlight on and pick a lane position that gives the best view of oncoming traffic. Provide a space cushion that gives you an escape path. When a driver is preparing to cross your path, slow and select a lane position that increases your visibility to that driver, and cover the clutch lever and both brakes to cut your reaction time. As you enter the intersection, move away from the vehicle. Do not change speed or position radically, because drivers may read that as a turn signal of sorts. Be prepared to brake hard and hold your position if an oncoming vehicle turns in front of you — and use this same strategy any time a vehicle in the oncoming lane is signalling a left turn, whether at an intersection or not.

At a blind intersection, move to the portion of the lane that brings you into the other driver's field of vision at the earliest possible moment. With a stop sign or stop line, stop there first, then edge forward and stop again just short of where the cross-traffic lane meets yours, lean forward and look around whatever is blocking the view — keeping your front wheel out of the cross lane while you look.
lessons.whyItMatters:
This is the highest-value topic in the manual. More than half of motorcycle-car crashes start here, and the single most common one is a driver turning left across a rider's path. Riders who believe eye contact protects them ride into that crash with confidence.

The exam draws heavily from this section, and the questions tend to test the counter-intuitive parts: eye contact does not mean you were seen, and the response to a threat is to slow and cover the controls rather than to accelerate through.
lessons.example: You are approaching a green light. A car in the oncoming lane is stopped with its left indicator on, and the driver appears to look straight at you. You do not treat that as permission. You slow, move to the lane position that shows you most clearly to that driver, cover the clutch and both brakes, and keep an escape path open on your right. If the car turns across you, your reaction has already been shortened to a squeeze and a press rather than a search for the levers. The manual asks you to use this same response whenever a vehicle in the oncoming lane signals a left turn — at an intersection or not.

lessons.plainEnglish:
From ahead or behind, a motorcycle's outline is much smaller than a car's — and it is difficult to see something you are not looking for, which is what most drivers are doing about motorcycles. Even when a driver does see you, smaller vehicles appear farther away than they actually are, so drivers pull out thinking they have plenty of time. The manual's blunt strategy is to pretend you are invisible, which keeps you in a hyper-aware mindset.

What you can change: clothing, lights and position. Most crashes occur during daylight hours, so bright-coloured clothing is a daylight tool, not a night one — bright orange, red, yellow or green jackets and vests are the best bets, and a brightly coloured helmet helps too, since your body is half the visible surface area of the rider and motorcycle together. Reflective material adds night visibility on top of that. Keep the headlight on at all times: during the day a motorcycle with its light on is twice as likely to be noticed, and low beam is used at night and in fog.

Communication comes from signals and the brake light. Use signals any time you plan to change lanes or turn, even when you think no one else is around, because the blinking light itself makes you easier to spot — then make sure the signal is cancelled after the turn, or a driver may pull into your path expecting you to turn again. Because a motorcycle's brake light is usually not as noticeable as a car's, flash it before slowing more quickly than expected, before slowing where others would not expect it, when stopped at an intersection with traffic approaching from behind, and when you are being followed closely.

Behind you is mirrors plus head checks. Check mirrors when stopped at an intersection, before changing lanes, and before slowing. Most motorcycle mirrors are convex: they give a wider view but make cars seem farther away than they really are. Mirrors alone are not enough, because motorcycles have blind spots — turn your head and look before changing lanes, checking the far lane as well as the one next to you.

At night, reduce speed, open up a three-second following distance or more, use the headlights of the car ahead to read the road, use your high beam whenever you are not following or meeting a car, wear reflective materials, and never override your headlight — do not let your total stopping distance exceed the distance your light beam illuminates.
lessons.whyItMatters:
The most common thing a driver says after hitting a motorcycle is that they never saw it. Everything in this topic is an attempt to move you out of that sentence. None of it is expensive and none of it requires skill; it is all decisions about gear, switches and position.

The exam likes the bright-clothing-in-daylight point in particular, because it feels counter-intuitive. Reflective material is the night tool; bright colour is the daylight tool, and most crashes happen in daylight.
lessons.example: You are riding a two-lane road in the afternoon in a bright yellow jacket with your headlight on. Ahead, a driver waits to pull out of a car park. You do not assume they will see you, so you also move to the lane position that puts you most clearly in their view. Later you plan to turn off at an unmarked farm track halfway down a block — somewhere no driver would expect anyone to slow — so you flash your brake light before you slow, signal early, and check your mirror and then turn your head before moving over. Once through the turn you check the signal has cancelled, because a signal left blinking invites the driver behind to pull into the space you are still using.

source.sourceQuote: A primary cause of single-vehicle crashes is motorcyclists running wide in a curve or turn.

lessons.plainEnglish:
No matter how careful you are, there will be times when you find yourself in a tight spot, and your chances then depend on two skills: stopping and swerving. Deciding which one the situation needs is part of the skill, because it is not always possible to stop quickly enough to avoid an obstacle.

The manual names the two mistakes crash-involved riders make. First, they underbrake the front tire and overbrake the rear — exactly backwards, since the front provides 70% or more of the stopping power. Second, they either fail to separate braking from swerving, or fail to choose swerving when swerving was the right answer.

A quick stop is both brakes at the same time, the front squeezed firmly and progressively rather than grabbed. If the front wheel locks, release the front brake lever immediately and reapply firmly with less pressure — front-wheel skids cause immediate loss of steering control and balance, and failing to fully release the lever immediately will result in a crash. The rear behaves differently: if you accidentally lock the rear brake on a good traction surface you can keep it locked until you have completely stopped, because even with a locked rear wheel you can control the motorcycle if it is upright and going in a straight line. What you must not do is release a locked rear wheel that has gone out of alignment with the front — the motorcycle can abruptly snap upright and throw the rider into the air ahead of it, which is a high-side crash.

In a curve, straighten and square the handlebars first, then stop. If that is impossible — there is a danger of running off the road in a left-hand curve, or oncoming traffic in a right-hand curve — brake smoothly and gradually, reducing lean and increasing brake pressure as traction returns. Always straighten the handlebars in the last few feet of stopping.

A swerve is a sudden change of direction: press the handgrip on the side of your intended escape, keep your body upright, let the motorcycle lean underneath you, and make your escape path the target of your vision. Press the opposite handgrip once clear to come back. And if the situation allows, separate braking from swerving — brake before or after, never while making an aggressive swerve.
lessons.whyItMatters:
This topic is where the exam stops asking what you know and starts asking what you would do. Every question has an intuitive wrong answer: grab the front brake, hold a locked front wheel, brake in the middle of a swerve, brake hard while leaned over. Each of those is the crash.

The front-versus-rear skid distinction is the single most valuable pair of facts here: release a locked front wheel immediately, but a locked rear on good traction and in a straight line can stay locked until you stop.
lessons.example: A car pulls out of a side road and stops across your lane. You are close. There is not enough room to stop, so this is a swerve, not a brake. You press the handgrip on the side of the gap you intend to use, keep your body upright and let the motorcycle lean underneath you, eyes on the escape path rather than on the car. Once you are past the car you press the opposite handgrip to straighten up — and only then, on a straight and upright motorcycle, do you brake. Braking in the middle of the swerve would have spent the traction you needed to change direction.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Relax, maintain a steady speed and ride straight across.

lessons.plainEnglish:
Four kinds of surface raise your chance of falling: uneven surfaces and obstacles, slippery surfaces, railroad tracks, and grooves and gratings. Each has its own answer, and the answers are not interchangeable.

For obstacles, the first choice is to avoid them by slowing or going around. If you must go over a smaller one, approach it as close to a 90 degree angle as possible, slow down as much as you can before contact, make sure the motorcycle is straight, rise slightly off the seat with your weight on the footrests so your knees and elbows absorb the shock, and just before contact roll on the throttle slightly to lighten the front end, then roll off. Afterwards, pull off the road and check your tires and rims for damage before riding any farther.

Slippery surfaces include wet pavement — particularly just after it starts to rain, before surface oil washes to the side — gravel, sand, mud, leaves, snow and ice, and painted lane markings, steel plates and surface covers, especially when wet. The technique is: reduce speed before you reach the slippery surface, avoid sudden changes of speed or direction, and use both brakes, because the front brake is still effective on a slippery surface — just squeeze it gradually. When rain starts, ride in the tire tracks left by vehicles rather than the centre of the lane, and watch for oil spots when you put a foot down. Ice tends to form in low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses, and dirt and gravel collect along the sides of the road, especially on curves and ramps.

Tracks are counter-intuitive. It is usually safer to ride straight within your lane to cross railroad or trolley tracks — turning to take them at 90 degrees can put you into another lane of traffic. The 45 degree rule applies to a different thing: tracks, ruts or pavement seams that run parallel to your path, which you move away from and then cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees with a deliberate turn.

Rain grooves and bridge gratings make a motorcycle weave, and that uneasy wandering feeling is generally not hazardous. Relax, hold a steady speed and ride straight across. Crossing at an angle forces riders to zigzag to stay in the lane, and the zigzag is far more hazardous than the wandering feeling.
lessons.whyItMatters:
This topic contains two rules that look like each other and mean opposite things: cross railroad tracks by riding straight within your lane, but cross parallel seams at at least 45 degrees. Riders who remember only 'an angle' apply the wrong one and steer into the next lane.

The grating rule is similar. The weave feels dangerous and is not; the correction people instinctively make — zigzagging to hold the lane — is the dangerous part.
lessons.example: You are riding into town as the first rain in weeks begins to fall. That is the worst moment for traction, because surface oil has not yet washed to the side of the road. You slow before reaching the wet section rather than on it, move out of the centre of the lane and into the tire tracks left by cars, and keep every input smooth. Approaching a level crossing that runs diagonally across the road, you resist the urge to turn and square it up — turning to take tracks at 90 degrees could put you into oncoming traffic — and instead ride straight within your lane. On the bridge beyond, the grating makes the motorcycle wander; you relax, hold a steady speed and ride straight across.

source.sourceQuote: When the engine “locks” or “freezes” it is usually low on oil.

lessons.plainEnglish:
Mechanical failures on a motorcycle become control problems instantly, so each one has a first response worth knowing before you need it.

Tire failure is rarely heard — it is felt. If the motorcycle starts handling differently, suspect a tire. A front tire going down makes the steering feel heavy; a rear one makes the back of the motorcycle jerk or sway from side to side. Either way: hold the handgrips firmly, ease off the throttle, and keep a straight course. If braking is required, gradually apply the brake of the tire that is not flat, if you are sure which one it is. When the motorcycle slows, edge to the side of the road, squeeze the clutch and stop.

A stuck throttle is first treated by twisting it back and forth several times, which may free a sticking cable. If it stays stuck, immediately operate the engine cut-off switch and squeeze the clutch lever at the same time. That removes power from the rear wheel even though engine sound may not immediately decline. Move to a safe area and stop, then find the cause before riding again.

A wobble is the front wheel and handlebars suddenly shaking side to side at any speed. Most wobbles trace to improper loading, unsuitable accessories or incorrect tire pressure. The response is counter-intuitive: do not try to accelerate out of it, which only makes the motorcycle more unstable, and do not brake, which could make the wobble worse. Instead grip the handlebars firmly without fighting the wobble, close the throttle gradually, move your weight as far forward and down as possible, and pull off the road as soon as you can.

Drive train failure is rare with routine maintenance, but a chain or belt that slips or breaks could lock the rear wheel and cause a skid. If it breaks you will notice an instant loss of power to the rear wheel: close the throttle and brake to a stop in a safe area. Engine seizure is usually caused by low oil — the first sign is a loss of engine power or a change in the engine's sound. Squeeze the clutch lever to disengage the engine from the rear wheel, pull off the road and stop, and check the oil.
lessons.whyItMatters:
Every one of these has a wrong instinct attached to it. Braking on a flat tire, braking or accelerating in a wobble, hunting for the ignition key instead of the cut-off switch, riding on after an engine note changes. The manual's answers are short and specific enough to memorise, and the exam asks them almost verbatim.

The common thread is also worth seeing: in nearly every case the first action is to remove power smoothly — close the throttle or squeeze the clutch — rather than to brake.
lessons.example: You are on a dual carriageway when the steering starts to feel heavy and vague. You did not hear anything, but the handling has changed, so you treat it as a tire failure. You hold the handgrips firmly, ease off the throttle rather than braking, and keep a straight course while the speed falls. You are confident it is the front, so if you need to slow further you use the rear brake gradually. As the motorcycle slows you edge to the side of the road, squeeze the clutch and stop well clear of the traffic lane.

lessons.plainEnglish:
You should do everything you safely can to avoid hitting an animal — but the manual attaches a hard limit to that. If you are in traffic, remain in your lane, because hitting something small is less dangerous to you than hitting something big, like a car. A swerve into another lane to miss a squirrel is how riders are hit by vehicles.

Dogs get their own treatment, because motorcycles seem to attract them. If you are being chased, downshift and approach the animal slowly; as you approach it, accelerate and leave the animal behind. Do not kick at the animal — keep control of the motorcycle and look where you want to go. Larger animals are handled in the opposite way: for deer, elk or cattle, brake and prepare to stop, because they are unpredictable.

Flying objects — insects, cigarettes thrown from cars, pebbles kicked up by the vehicle ahead — can smear or crack face protection, or strike you in the eye, face or mouth without it. Whatever happens, keep your eyes on the road and your hands on the handlebars, then pull off the road and repair the damage when safe.

Leaving the road, whether to check the motorcycle or just to rest, has four steps. Check the roadside is firm enough to ride on — if it is soft grass, loose sand or you are simply unsure, slow way down before turning onto it. Signal clearly, because drivers behind will not expect you to slow, and check your mirror and make a head check first. Pull off the road, getting as far off as you can, since a motorcycle by the roadside is hard to spot and you do not want someone else pulling off in the same place. And park carefully, because loose and sloped shoulders make setting the side or centre stand difficult.
lessons.whyItMatters:
The animal rules are where good instincts get riders hurt. Swerving to avoid something small, or kicking at a dog, both trade a minor impact for a loss of control or a collision with a vehicle. The manual's ranking is explicit and it is the answer the exam wants.

Leaving the road is also underrated. A rider dealing with a mechanical problem is already distracted, and the shoulder is exactly where the surface is loose and the traffic does not expect them.
lessons.example: A dog runs out and starts chasing you along a suburban street. You resist the urge to swerve or kick out. You downshift and approach it slowly so it commits to a line, and as you reach it you accelerate away and leave it behind, keeping your eyes on where you want to go. Half a mile later a deer steps out of a hedge — a different animal and a different rule. This one gets braking and preparation to stop, because larger animals are unpredictable and hitting one at speed is not a minor impact.

source.sourceQuote: Fasten the load securely with elastic cords (bungee cords or nets).

lessons.plainEnglish:
A passenger or a large load changes how the motorcycle handles, which is why the manual says only experienced riders should attempt it. Before you go, prepare the machine: check tire pressures against the owner's manual for the load, adjust suspension settings if needed, and re-aim the headlight, which the extra weight lifts.

The equipment list is short and non-negotiable. The passenger needs the same level of personal protective gear as you. The motorcycle needs passenger footrests, a seat large enough to hold both of you without crowding, and a strap or solid handholds. A child goes immediately behind the rider, never in front — a child sitting in front cannot properly balance and may interfere with your control.

Then instruct the passenger, every time, even if they ride themselves. Get on only after you have started the engine and have the transmission in neutral, while you keep both feet down and the front brake applied. Sit as far forward as possible without hindering your control. Hold firmly onto your waist, hips, belt or the handholds. Keep both feet firmly on the footrests, even when stopped, because firm footing prevents a passenger falling off and pulling you off with them. Keep legs away from the muffler, chains and moving parts. Stay directly behind you and lean with you through turns and curves. Avoid unnecessary conversation and sudden moves. Rise slightly off the seat when crossing an obstacle, and tighten their hold when you approach bumps, move off, or turn sharply.

Riding changes too. The heavier your passenger, the longer it may take to speed up, slow down or turn. Ride a little slower, especially through curves, corners and bumps; start slowing earlier as you approach a stop and keep a larger space cushion; and wait for larger gaps to cross, enter or merge in traffic.

Cargo has its own physics. Place the load over or in front of the rear axle — loads mounted behind it affect how the motorcycle turns and brakes and can cause a wobble. Keep loads low or in saddlebags, because a high load raises the centre of gravity and upsets balance. Load saddlebags with about the same weight each, since an uneven load pulls the motorcycle to one side and an overloaded bag can catch in the wheel or chain and lock the rear wheel. Fasten loads with elastic cords, ideally with more than one attachment point per side; rope can stretch and knots can come loose. Stop and check the load often.
lessons.whyItMatters:
A passenger is a second life on your machine and a substantial change to its behaviour, and most of the failures are preparation failures rather than riding failures — no footrests, no handhold, no briefing, a load strapped behind the axle with rope.

The exam favours three points here: passengers lean with you, a child goes behind the rider, and loads go over or in front of the rear axle.
lessons.example: You are taking a friend across town on the back for the first time. Before setting off you check both tire pressures for the extra weight, confirm the bike has passenger footrests and a grab strap, and see that your friend has the same standard of helmet, jacket, gloves and boots that you do. You brief them: get on only once the engine is running and the bike is in neutral while you hold the front brake with both feet down; hold your waist; keep both feet on the footrests even at traffic lights; lean with you, not against you. On the road you ride a little slower, start braking earlier for every junction, and wait for a bigger gap than usual before pulling out.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Passengers, Cargo and Group Riding
source.sourceQuote: Intersections present the highest risk for motorcyclists in a group.

lessons.plainEnglish:
A group ride starts before the engines do. Hold a rider's meeting to agree the route, the length of riding segments, rest stops and the locations for fuel, meals and lodging, so that a rider who becomes separated does not have to hurry to catch up. Choose a lead rider and a sweep rider, both of whom should be the most experienced riders in the group; the sweep rider is last and sets the pace. Inexperienced riders go just behind the leader, so they never have to chase the group and the experienced riders behind can watch them.

Three rules matter most: no competition, no passing of other riders and no tailgating. If a rider insists on riding faster than the group, let them go ahead to an agreed meeting point rather than letting the group chase them.

Spacing is a staggered formation: the leader in the left side of the lane, the second rider at least one second back in the right side, the third in the left position at least two seconds behind the first, and so on. That keeps ranks close while giving every rider room to react. Never ride directly alongside another rider in the same lane — there is no place to go if you have to avoid a car or a hazard. Move to single file in curves, when turning, and when entering or leaving freeways.

Intersections present the highest risk for motorcyclists in a group. When making a left turn at a signal with a turn arrow, tighten the formation to get as many riders through as possible, but make the turn single file — not side by side. If not all riders get through the light, those left behind stop at a safe point ahead and wait, so nobody feels pressured to speed up or run a red light.

Passing in formation depends on the road. On a freeway or interstate the group may pass as a unit. On a two-lane highway, riders in a staggered formation pass one at a time: the lead rider pulls out when safe and continues at passing speed to open room for the next, and each following rider judges the oncoming traffic independently — just because the lead rider passed does not mean it is still safe for you.
lessons.whyItMatters:
A group multiplies the consequences of one rider's error, and it introduces pressures that do not exist when you ride alone: the urge to keep up, to close a gap, or to follow the rider in front through a light that has changed.

The formation details are exam material — leader on the left, second rider one second back on the right, third at least two seconds behind the leader — and so is the two-lane passing rule, because it contradicts the instinct to follow the rider ahead through the gap.
lessons.example: Six of you set out on a two-lane road. At the meeting you agreed the route and the lunch stop, and put the two most experienced riders at the front and the back, with the newest rider second in line. You run a staggered formation: the leader left, the new rider one second back on the right, you two seconds behind the leader on the left. Approaching a slow lorry, nobody moves as a block. The leader passes when they have a clear view, then holds passing speed on the left to open room. The second rider moves up to the left position and waits for their own clear view — because conditions have changed since the leader went, and their pass has to be judged on its own.

lessons.plainEnglish:
Alcohol and drugs degrade your ability to think clearly and ride skilfully more than any other factor, and as little as one drink can have a significant effect on performance. Nearly a third of all fatally injured motorcycle riders had BAC levels above the legal limit of 0.08%, and another 8% had lower levels — evidence that a drink or two is enough to impair riding skill. The consequences are worse on a motorcycle: injuries occur in 90% of motorcycle crashes involving substance abuse, against 33% of automobile crashes.

Alcohol works fast because it does not need to be digested. Within minutes of being consumed it reaches the brain, and its major effect is to slow down and impair bodily functions, both mental and physical. BAC — Blood Alcohol Concentration — is the amount of alcohol in relation to blood in the body, and three primary factors determine it: how much you consume, how fast you drink, and your body weight. Other factors, including sex, physical condition and food intake, can push it higher still.

Two arithmetic facts matter. First, a 12-ounce beer, a mixed drink with a 1.5-ounce shot, and a 5-ounce glass of wine all contain the same amount of alcohol, so 'I only had a beer' is not a defence. Second, alcohol is eliminated at almost one drink per hour, so anything faster accumulates: two drinks in an hour leaves at least one in your bloodstream at the end of it, and seven drinks over three hours leaves at least four, needing four more hours to clear.

The law sets 0.08% for adults in all but one state, and 0.00 to 0.02% for operators under 21 depending on the state. But whether you are legally intoxicated is not the real issue: impairment of judgment and skills begins well below the legal limit. Worse, your ability to judge how well you are riding is affected first, so you ride more and more poorly while feeling you are doing better and better.

The choices are simple. Do not drink, since your resistance weakens once you start and setting a limit is a poor alternative at best. Or do not ride: leave the motorcycle so you are not tempted, and wait until your system has eliminated the alcohol and its fatiguing after-effects. For friends who have had too much, step in — arrange a safe ride, slow the pace of drinking, keep them there with food and coffee, take their key if you can, and use peer pressure from a group of friends.

Cannabis, legal or not where you are, distorts your perception of time, space and speed — exactly the judgments a rider makes continuously. Smoked, its effects begin within minutes and last 2 to 4 hours; eaten, the onset may be delayed more than an hour and the effects last more than 6. Riders impaired by cannabis can be convicted of riding under the influence and face similar harsh penalties. Fatigue is the last impairment: riding is more tiring than driving, so protect yourself from wind, cold and rain, limit your distance — experienced riders seldom ride more than about six hours a day — stop and get off the motorcycle at least every two hours, and avoid stimulants, which leave extreme fatigue or depression when they wear off.
lessons.whyItMatters:
This topic carries the heaviest consequences of anything in the manual, and it is heavily represented on the exam because the numbers are precise and testable: 0.08%, 0.00 to 0.02% under 21, one drink per hour, three drink equivalents, 2 to 4 hours smoked and over 6 hours eaten.

The conceptual point matters as much as the numbers. Legal and safe are not the same thing. Impairment begins well below 0.08%, and the first thing impaired is your ability to notice you are impaired.
lessons.example: You have four drinks over two hours at a friend's house. Elimination runs at almost one drink per hour, so at the end of the two hours at least two drinks are still in your system — and you would need at least two more hours before you could consider riding. Waiting one hour and 'feeling fine' does not help, because your ability to judge how well you are riding was the first thing affected. The honest options are the manual's two: do not drink, or do not ride. You leave the motorcycle where it is and arrange another way home.

Laces should be left long so boots can be removed quickly
questions.explanation: Boots or shoes should be high and sturdy enough to cover your ankles and give them support, with hard, durable, slip-resistant soles and short heels that will not catch on rough surfaces. Laces get tucked in so they cannot catch on the motorcycle.
choiceExplanations: Coverage and ankle support are the stated requirements, which a low closed-toe shoe does not meet.
The manual says to keep heels short so they do not catch on rough surfaces.
Laces should be tucked in so they will not catch on the motorcycle.

questions.question: Which material does the manual say offers the most protection in riding clothing?
choices: Leather
Denim
Nylon mesh
Cotton canvas
questions.explanation: The manual states that leather offers the most protection, and adds that sturdy synthetic material provides a lot of protection as well. Either way, jacket and pants should cover the arms and legs completely and fit snugly enough to keep from flapping in the wind.
choiceExplanations: Denim is not named; the manual ranks leather first and sturdy synthetics close behind.
Mesh is not the protective ranking the manual gives, though synthetics can provide a lot of protection.
Cotton canvas is not identified as a protective riding material.

questions.question: Why does the manual recommend wearing a jacket even in warm weather?
choices: To prevent dehydration
To satisfy state helmet law
To reduce wind noise
To make the bike easier to handle
questions.explanation: The manual advises wearing a jacket even in warm weather to prevent dehydration, noting that many jackets are designed to protect without overheating you on summer days. Clothing also protects from heat, cold, debris and the hot and moving parts of the motorcycle.
choiceExplanations: Helmet law concerns head protection; it says nothing about jackets.
Wind noise is handled by hearing protection, not by a jacket.
Clothing does not change how the motorcycle handles.

questions.question: How does the manual describe a motorcycle that fits you?
choices: Your feet reach the ground while seated and the controls are easy to operate
You can hold it upright with one hand while seated
The seat height is at least 32 inches
It weighs less than 400 pounds
questions.explanation: The manual's fit test has two parts: your feet should reach the ground while you are seated on the motorcycle, and the controls should be easy to operate. It adds that smaller motorcycles are usually easier for beginners to operate.
choiceExplanations: No one-hand test appears in the manual's fit description.
The manual gives no seat-height figure; never assume a number it does not state.
No weight limit is given as a measure of fit.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed as minimum equipment for a street-legal motorcycle?

Turn signals
Two mirrors
Front and rear brakes
questions.explanation: The manual's minimum list for a street-legal motorcycle is a headlight, taillight and brake light; front and rear brakes; turn signals; a horn; and two mirrors. A tachometer is not among them.
choiceExplanations: Turn signals are on the manual's minimum equipment list.
Two mirrors are on the minimum equipment list.
Front and rear brakes are on the minimum equipment list.

questions.question: What does the manual say about the riders involved in more than half of all crashes?
choices: They have under five months of experience on that particular motorcycle
They have been riding for more than ten years
They are riding without a valid endorsement
They are riding machines with engines larger than 750cc
questions.explanation: The manual states that more than half of all crashes involve riders with less than five months of experience on their motorcycle. The measure is experience on that particular machine, which is why it warns to ride extra carefully on any motorcycle that is new or unfamiliar to you.
choiceExplanations: Long experience is not what the statistic describes; recent unfamiliarity is.
The manual ties the figure to experience on the machine, not to licensing status.
No engine size appears anywhere in the statistic.

questions.question: You borrow a friend's motorcycle. What does the manual say to do before riding it in traffic?
choices: Get familiar with it away from traffic and locate every control without looking
Ride it briefly in traffic at low speed to learn its handling
Adjust the suspension to your own weight before moving it
Nothing special, provided you already hold an endorsement
questions.explanation: The manual says that if you borrow a motorcycle, get familiar with it away from traffic, and to find the turn signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel-supply valve and engine cut-off switch and operate them without having to look. Riding an unfamiliar motorcycle adds risk, and most crashes involve riders with under five months on their machine.
choiceExplanations: Learning an unfamiliar bike in traffic is the exact risk the manual tells you to remove first.
Suspension adjustment is advised for carrying loads or passengers, not as the borrowing step.
Holding an endorsement does not remove the unfamiliarity risk the manual warns about.

questions.question: How often does the manual say a pre-ride inspection should be done?
choices: Before every ride
Once a week
Once a month
Before long trips only
questions.explanation: A pre-ride inspection only takes a few minutes and should be done before every ride to prevent problems. The manual compares it to checking the weather forecast — routine and automatic — because a minor failure that merely inconveniences a driver can put a rider on the road surface.
choiceExplanations: Weekly is the stated interval for brake fluid and coolant, not for the whole inspection.
A monthly interval appears nowhere; the inspection belongs to every ride.
The manual applies it to every ride, not only to long ones.

questions.question: T-CLOCS is the manual's reminder for what?

The four steps of a turn
The three-step SEE strategy
The staggered formation used in group riding
questions.explanation: T-CLOCS is the MSF's pre-ride inspection reminder, and the manual says a T-CLOCS inspection should be conducted before every ride. The letters stand for Tires and wheels, Controls, Lights and electrics, Oil and other fluids, Chassis, and Stands.
choiceExplanations: The four steps of a turn are SLOW, LOOK, PRESS and ROLL.
SEE stands for Search, Evaluate and Execute, a separate strategy.
Staggered formation is a group-riding spacing pattern with no checklist acronym.

questions.question: During the controls check, what should the throttle do when you release it?
choices: Snap back to fully closed
Stay where you left it until you close it by hand
Return slowly to about a quarter open
Hold engine speed steady at idle plus 1,000 rpm
questions.explanation: Under C for Controls, the manual says to make sure the clutch and throttle operate smoothly, and that the throttle should snap back to fully closed when released. A throttle that does not is the same fault that later appears as the 'stuck throttle' emergency.
choiceExplanations: A throttle that holds its position is a stuck throttle, which the manual treats as an emergency.
Partial return is a fault, not the expected behaviour.
No such rpm behaviour is described; the check is simply that the throttle closes fully.

questions.question: Why does the manual tell you to clean and adjust mirrors before starting out?
choices: It is difficult to ride with one hand while you try to adjust a mirror
Mirrors cannot be adjusted once the engine is warm
Adjusting mirrors while moving is illegal
A moving motorcycle's vibration prevents accurate adjustment
questions.explanation: The manual's reason is practical: clean and adjust mirrors before starting, because it is difficult to ride with one hand while you try to adjust a mirror. Each mirror should be set so you can see the lane behind and the lane next to you — the road behind and to the side is what matters, not your own shoulder.
choiceExplanations: Engine temperature has nothing to do with mirror adjustment.
The manual gives a practical reason, not a legal one.
Vibration is not the reason given; riding one-handed is.

questions.question: What assumption does the manual say a rider must make about other drivers?
choices: You cannot be sure they will see you or yield the right of way
They will see you if your headlight is on
They will yield once eye contact is made
They will behave predictably in daylight
questions.explanation: The manual is explicit: as a rider you cannot be sure that other operators will see you or yield the right of way. Everything else in the book — conspicuity, space cushion, SEE, covering the controls — is built on that assumption rather than on other people's good behaviour.
choiceExplanations: A headlight makes you twice as likely to be noticed during the day, but it is not a guarantee.
The manual says never to count on eye contact — a driver can look straight at you and not see you.
Daylight is when most crashes occur; it does not make other drivers predictable.

questions.question: A driver runs a yellow light turning red and collides with you as you pull out on green. How does the manual frame responsibility?
choices: It was the driver's responsibility to stop and your responsibility to look before moving out
Responsibility rests entirely with the driver who ran the light
Responsibility rests with you, because you entered the intersection
It is an accident — an unforeseen event without fault
questions.explanation: This is the manual's own example. It concludes that it was the driver's responsibility to stop, and it was your responsibility to look before moving out. Someone else may start the chain of events, but that does not leave any of us free of our responsibility to reduce risk — and blame does not matter when someone is injured.
choiceExplanations: The manual refuses to place all responsibility on the other party, even when they broke the rule.
The manual does not shift the whole burden to the rider either; both had a duty.
The manual expressly rejects calling traffic crashes accidents, since they rarely occur without fault.

questions.question: How far ahead does the manual say to search your path of travel?
choices: 12 seconds
4 seconds
2 seconds
20 seconds
questions.explanation: Among the things that lessen your chances of a crash, the manual lists searching your path of travel 12 seconds ahead. That long look gives you time to prepare for a situation before it becomes urgent, while the 4-second and 2-second distances handle what is already close.
choiceExplanations: Four seconds is the immediate or urgent path, not the long search distance.
Two seconds is the minimum following distance, a different measurement.
Twenty seconds is not a figure the manual uses.

questions.question: A rider scans only as far ahead as the vehicle directly in front. Which lead time are they missing?
choices: The 12-second search of the path of travel
The 2-second following distance
The half-second reaction allowance
The 30-second route plan
questions.explanation: The manual describes three lead times: at least a 2-second following distance, a 4-second immediate path, and a search out to an area it would take about 12 seconds to reach. A rider watching only the vehicle ahead has the short gap covered and has lost the 12-second look that would let them prepare before a problem becomes urgent.
choiceExplanations: Watching the vehicle directly ahead is roughly the 2-second gap; that is the part they are doing.
No half-second reaction allowance is defined in the manual.
There is no 30-second figure in the manual's lead times.

questions.question: Which of these does the manual list as a way to lessen your chances of a crash?
choices: Communicate your intentions with signals, brake light and lane position
Ride slightly above the flow of traffic to stay ahead of it
Stay in the centre of a lane at all times
Rely on eye contact to confirm a driver has seen you
questions.explanation: The manual's list is: be visible, communicate your intentions, maintain an adequate space cushion, search your path of travel 12 seconds ahead, identify and separate hazards, and be prepared to act. Communicating intentions means using the proper signals, brake light and lane position.
choiceExplanations: Riding above the traffic flow is nowhere recommended; speed is not listed as a safety measure.
Lane position should change as traffic situations change, not stay fixed in the centre.
The manual says never count on eye contact — a driver can look at you and still not see you.

questions.question: What does the manual mean by 'be visible'?
choices: Wear proper clothing, use your headlight, and ride in the best lane position to see and be seen
Ride only during daylight hours
Stay directly beside other vehicles so drivers can see you
Use your horn continuously in traffic
questions.explanation: Under 'be visible' the manual names three things together: wear proper clothing, use your headlight, and ride in the best lane position to see and be seen. Visibility is something you arrange, not something you hope other drivers supply.
choiceExplanations: Daylight is when most crashes occur; visibility is about gear, lights and position, not time of day.
Riding alongside other vehicles puts you in blind spots and blocks your escape route.
The horn is for getting attention in specific situations, and is not as loud as a car's.

questions.question: Where should your knees be while riding?
choices: Against the gas tank
Spread wide for balance
Tucked behind the footrests
Resting on the engine cases
questions.explanation: The manual says to keep your knees against the gas tank to help you keep your balance as the motorcycle turns. That contact point, together with feet firmly on the footrests, is what lets your lower body hold position while your hands work the controls.
choiceExplanations: Spreading the knees removes the contact that helps hold you steady as the motorcycle turns.
Knees cannot reach behind the footrests, and feet belong firmly on the footrests themselves.
Resting on hot engine cases is neither possible for balance nor safe.

questions.question: How far forward should you sit on the seat?
choices: Far enough forward that your arms are slightly bent on the handgrips
As far back as the seat allows, for comfort
Far enough forward that your arms are straight
Directly over the rear axle
questions.explanation: The manual says to sit far enough forward so that your arms are slightly bent when you hold the handgrips, because bending your arms permits you to press on the handlebars without having to reach too far. Pressing the handgrip is exactly how you make the motorcycle lean and turn.
choiceExplanations: Sitting far back forces you to reach, which the manual's seating rule is written to avoid.
Straight arms prevent you pressing on the handlebars, which is how the motorcycle is steered.
Load placement relates to the rear axle; rider position is set by arm bend at the handgrips.

questions.question: Why does the manual warn against letting your toes point downward?
choices: They may get caught between the road and the footrests
It reduces the grip of the rear brake pedal
It shifts weight too far back on the motorcycle
It makes the clutch harder to feather
questions.explanation: The manual warns that if your toes point downward they may get caught between the road and the footrests. Feet stay firmly on the footrests, near the controls, and are never dragged — a foot catching on something can injure you and cost you control.
choiceExplanations: Rear brake grip is not affected by toe angle; the hazard is contact with the road.
Toe angle does not meaningfully change weight distribution.
The clutch is a hand lever on most motorcycles and is unrelated to foot position.

questions.question: Where is the gearshift lever and how is it operated?
choices: In front of the left footrest, operated by the left foot
In front of the right footrest, operated by the right foot
On the left handlebar, operated by hand
Behind the left footrest, operated by the heel
questions.explanation: The manual states that the gearshift lever is located in front of the left footrest and is operated by the left foot. Lift and release to shift up a gear; press down and release to shift down. Each lift or press changes exactly one gear.
choiceExplanations: The right foot works the rear brake pedal, not the gearshift.
The left hand works the clutch lever; shifting is a foot control.
The lever sits in front of the footrest and is lifted or pressed with the toe.

questions.question: To shift up to a higher gear, what do you do with the shift lever?
choices: Position your foot under it, then lift and release
Press it down and release
Hold it up until the next gear engages
Press it down twice in quick succession
questions.explanation: The manual says that to shift up to a higher gear you position your foot under the shift lever and lift and release. Spring loading returns the lever to centre so the mechanism resets for the next shift. The full upshift is a three-step process: roll off the throttle as you squeeze the clutch, lift the lever firmly, then smoothly ease out the clutch and adjust the throttle.
choiceExplanations: Pressing down and releasing is the downshift, not the upshift.
The lever is spring-loaded and returns to centre; holding it does nothing further.
Each press changes one gear down, so two presses would drop two gears.

questions.question: What happens if you shift into a lower gear while still travelling too fast?
choices: The motorcycle will lurch and the rear wheel may skid
The engine will stall immediately
The transmission will refuse to select the gear
The front wheel will lift
questions.explanation: The manual warns to make certain you are riding slowly enough when you shift into a lower gear, because if not, the motorcycle will lurch and the rear wheel may skid. A sudden change in power to the rear wheel is a skid risk, which is why smooth clutch release matters most on downshifts.
choiceExplanations: A stall is not what the manual describes; the problem is a lurch and possible rear-wheel skid.
The gear does engage — that is precisely why the lurch happens.
The manual attributes no front-wheel lift to downshifting too early.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c

source.sourceQuote: Make certain you are riding slowly enough when you shift into a lower gear.

questions.question: You are riding downhill and need a lower gear. What does the manual say you may need to do first?
choices: Use the brakes to slow sufficiently before downshifting safely
Accelerate briefly to match engine speed
Shift two gears at once to compensate for the slope
Pull in the clutch and coast until the hill flattens
questions.explanation: The manual states that when riding downhill or shifting into first gear you may need to use the brakes to slow sufficiently before downshifting safely. Gravity is adding speed, so the brakes do the work the closed throttle would otherwise do before the lower gear is engaged.
choiceExplanations: Accelerating increases the speed mismatch the downshift is already struggling with.
Shifting through several gears at once is possible but does not solve being too fast for the gear.
Coasting with the clutch in removes engine braking exactly where a downhill needs it.

source.sourceQuote: Make certain you are riding slowly enough when you shift into a lower gear.

questions.question: What does the manual call the slowing effect produced by shifting to a lower gear?
choices: Engine braking
Compression locking
Linked braking
Trail braking
questions.explanation: The manual states that shifting to a lower gear causes an effect similar to using the brakes, and that this is known as engine braking. To use it, shift down one gear at a time and ease out the clutch lever through the friction zone between downshifts.
choiceExplanations: Compression locking is not a term the manual uses.
Linked braking is a hydraulic system connecting the front and rear brakes.
Trail braking does not appear in the manual.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: Shifting to a lower gear causes an effect similar to using the brakes. This is known as engine braking.

questions.question: A rider slowing for a junction shifts down one gear at a time, easing the clutch out between shifts. What are they using?
choices: Engine braking
Counterbalancing
Integrated braking
The friction-zone launch technique
questions.explanation: This is the manual's description of engine braking: shift down one gear at a time and ease out the clutch lever through the friction zone between each downshift, staying in the friction zone until engine speed stabilises. It supplements the brakes rather than replacing them.
choiceExplanations: Counterbalancing is a body-position technique for slow, tight turns.
Integrated braking is a hydraulic system that applies partial front brake with the rear.
No such technique is described; the friction zone is used here as part of engine braking.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: Shifting to a lower gear causes an effect similar to using the brakes. This is known as engine braking.

questions.question: How often does the manual say to use both brakes?
choices: Every time you slow or stop
Only in emergency stops
Only when the road surface is dry
Only when carrying a passenger or cargo
questions.explanation: The manual says to always use both brakes every time you slow or stop, and explains why: using both brakes for even normal stops will permit you to develop the proper skill of using both brakes properly in an emergency. The emergency is not the moment to try the front brake for the first time.
choiceExplanations: Reserving both brakes for emergencies is the habit the manual is written to prevent.
Both brakes are used on slippery surfaces too, with gentle, gradual pressure.
Load changes braking distance but does not change which brakes you use.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: Always use both brakes every time you slow or stop.

questions.question: Why does the manual insist on using both brakes even for routine stops?
choices: So the skill is developed and automatic when an emergency comes
Because using one brake wears the pads unevenly
Because the rear brake alone is illegal on public roads
Because the front brake overheats if used alone
questions.explanation: The reason is skill, not mechanics: using both brakes for even normal stops will permit you to develop the proper skill of using both brakes properly in an emergency. A rider who only ever uses the rear will reach for the rear under pressure, which is the pattern behind most crash-involved braking errors.
choiceExplanations: Pad wear is not the manual's reason; skill development is.
The manual states no such legal requirement about brake use.
No overheating warning is given for the front brake.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: Always use both brakes every time you slow or stop.

questions.question: Of a motorcycle's total stopping power, roughly how much is available at the front brake?
choices: 70% or more
Roughly a quarter of it
Roughly half of it
An equal share with the rear brake
questions.explanation: The manual states that the front brake is more powerful and can provide 70% or more of your total stopping power, and that it is safe to use if you use it properly. Weight transferring forward under braking is what gives the front tire that extra traction.
choiceExplanations: A quarter badly understates the front brake and is the belief behind under-braking the front.
Half is still an understatement; the manual's figure is 70% or more.
The front is the more powerful of the two, not an equal partner with the rear.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: The front brake is more powerful and can provide 70% or more of your total stopping power.

questions.question: How should the front brake be applied for a firm stop?
choices: Squeezed smoothly, firmly and with progressively more force
Grabbed hard at once to use all available traction
Applied in short repeated pulses
Applied only after the rear brake has locked
questions.explanation: The manual says to squeeze the front brake smoothly, firmly and with progressively more force, and not to grab the lever or use abrupt pressure. As weight transfers forward more traction becomes available at the front wheel, so the front brake can be applied more firmly after braking begins.
choiceExplanations: The manual warns not to grab the brake lever or use abrupt pressure — that is what locks the wheel.
Pulsing is what ABS does electronically; a rider squeezes progressively instead.
Locking the rear on purpose gives up directional control and is not a braking technique.

questions.question: Maximum straight-line braking is achieved by:
choices: Fully applying both front and rear brakes without locking either wheel
Applying the front brake only, as hard as possible
Locking the rear wheel and steering with the front
Downshifting through every gear while braking lightly
questions.explanation: The manual defines maximum straight-line braking as fully applying both front and rear brakes without locking either wheel. Keep your knees against the tank and your eyes up, looking well ahead, which helps you stop in a straight line and keeps lean angle out of the equation.
choiceExplanations: The rear brake still contributes, and front-only braking gives up part of the available stopping power.
A locked rear wheel removes your ability to change direction and risks a high-side crash.
Engine braking supplements the brakes; it is not how maximum braking is produced.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: Maximum straight-line braking is accomplished by fully applying both front and rear brakes without locking either wheel.

questions.question: During a maximum-effort stop, what should happen to rear brake pressure as the motorcycle slows?
choices: It should be light-to-lighter, because traction leaves the rear as weight transfers forward
It should increase steadily to match the front
It should be released entirely once the front is applied
It should be pulsed on and off about once a second
questions.explanation: The manual says to apply light-to-lighter pressure to the rear brake pedal to prevent a rear wheel skid, because as weight transfers forward less traction is available at the rear. The front gets firmer as braking continues; the rear gets lighter.
choiceExplanations: Increasing rear pressure as rear traction falls is precisely how riders lock the rear wheel.
Both brakes are used together; abandoning the rear gives up part of the stopping power.
Manual pulsing is not a technique the manual describes; ABS does that automatically.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: Apply light-to-lighter pressure to the rear brake pedal to prevent a rear wheel skid.

questions.question: What happens to the traction available for braking when the motorcycle is leaned over?
choices: It is reduced, and the greater the lean angle the more likely the tires are to lose traction
It is unchanged, since the same tires are on the same road
It increases, because more of the tire is in contact with the road
It is reduced at the front only, not the rear
questions.explanation: The manual states that any time a motorcycle is leaned over, the amount of traction available for braking is reduced, and the greater the lean angle, the more the possibility of the tires losing traction. Traction spent holding the corner is not available to stop you.
choiceExplanations: Lean angle changes how much of the tire's grip is being spent on cornering rather than stopping.
Contact patch area is not the governing factor; traction is being used for cornering instead.
The reduction applies to the motorcycle's traction generally, not to one wheel.

questions.question: You must stop as quickly as possible while in a curve and conditions allow it. What does the manual say to do first?
choices: Get the motorcycle as perpendicular to the road as possible, then brake
Brake hard immediately and correct the lean afterwards
Widen your line into the next lane to reduce lean angle
Downshift to first gear before touching the brakes
questions.explanation: The manual says that to stop as quickly and as safely as possible in a curve, and depending on road and traffic conditions, try to get the motorcycle as perpendicular to the road as possible, then brake. Standing it up restores the traction that lean angle was consuming.
choiceExplanations: Hard braking at full lean is exactly what the reduced traction cannot support.
Crossing into another lane trades a braking problem for a collision risk.
Aggressive downshifting adds a rear-wheel skid risk and does not restore braking traction.
