questions.question: What is an anti-lock braking system designed to do?
choices: Prevent wheel lock-up and avoid skids when stopping in panic situations
Shorten stopping distance on every surface by about half
Apply the front brake automatically when the rear is used
Keep the motorcycle upright during a swerve
questions.explanation: The manual states that ABS is designed to prevent wheel lock-up and avoid skids when stopping in panic situations. It operates when too much pressure is applied to either brake control, releasing and reapplying pressure to maintain maximum braking effectiveness while the controls remain applied.
choiceExplanations: The manual claims no fixed reduction in stopping distance for ABS.
That describes an integrated braking system, which is a different mechanism.
ABS acts on braking; it does not stabilise the motorcycle during a swerve.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: ABS is designed to prevent wheel lock-up and avoid skids when stopping in panic situations.

questions.question: How quickly can an ABS release and reapply brake pressure?
choices: More than 15 times per second
About twice per second
About 5 times per second
About 50 times per second
questions.explanation: The manual states that ABS is capable of releasing and reapplying pressure more than 15 times per second. That is far faster than a rider can modulate a lever, which is why the correct technique with ABS is to keep the brake controls applied rather than pumping them.
choiceExplanations: Twice a second is far slower than the manual's figure.
Five times per second understates the stated capability.
Fifty times per second overstates it; the manual says more than 15.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: ABS is capable of releasing and reapplying pressure more than 15 times per second.

questions.question: Which description matches an integrated braking system?
choices: Partial front braking is applied whenever the rear brake is activated
Both brakes release automatically when a wheel locks
The rear brake is disabled above a set speed
Braking force is shared equally between the wheels at all times
questions.explanation: The manual describes linked braking as connecting the front and rear brakes so that either control applies pressure to both, and defines an integrated braking system as a variation of the linked system in which partial front braking is applied whenever the rear brake is activated.
choiceExplanations: That is ABS, which detects possible lock-up and modulates pressure.
No system described in the manual disables a brake at speed.
A linked system applies both brakes from either control, but not with equal force by definition.

questions.question: What are the four steps of a turn, in order?
choices: SLOW, LOOK, PRESS, ROLL
LOOK, SLOW, ROLL, PRESS
PRESS, SLOW, LOOK, ROLL
SLOW, PRESS, ROLL, LOOK
questions.explanation: The manual's four steps are SLOW, LOOK, PRESS and ROLL. Reduce speed before the turn, look through the turn to where you want to go, press the handgrip to lean the motorcycle, then roll on the throttle to maintain or slightly increase speed. In practice the steps overlap, but the order is the point.
choiceExplanations: Speed must come off before the turn; looking through it comes after slowing.
Pressing to lean before slowing means entering the corner too fast, the classic error.
Looking through the turn belongs before the lean, not after the throttle is rolled on.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: SLOW - Reduce speed before the turn by closing the throttle and, if necessary, applying both brakes.

questions.question: In the LOOK step, what exactly should you turn?
choices: Just your head, keeping your eyes level with the horizon
Your head and shoulders together
Your whole upper body into the corner
Your eyes only, keeping your head straight ahead
questions.explanation: The manual's LOOK step says to look through the turn to where you want to go, turning just your head, not your shoulders, and keeping your eyes level with the horizon. Where you look is where the motorcycle goes, so looking at the exit rather than at the edge of the road is what keeps your line.
choiceExplanations: The manual says to turn just your head, not your shoulders.
Turning the upper body changes your weight on the motorcycle and is not what is instructed.
Eyes alone limit how far through the turn you can see; the head turns with them.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: LOOK - Look through the turn to where you want to go. Turn just your head, not your shoulders, and keep your eyes level with the horizon.

questions.question: To make the motorcycle go left in a turn, you:
choices: Press the left handgrip so the motorcycle leans left
Press the right handgrip so the motorcycle leans left
Pull the left handgrip toward you
Shift your weight left without touching the handgrips
questions.explanation: The manual states that to turn, the motorcycle must lean, and that to lean it you press on the handgrip in the direction of the turn: press left handgrip, lean left, go left. The higher the speed or the sharper the turn, the greater the lean angle needs to be.
choiceExplanations: Pressing the right handgrip leans the motorcycle right and takes you right.
The instruction is to press on the handgrip, not to pull it.
The manual's steering instruction is a handgrip press; body weight alone is not how the lean is initiated.

questions.question: A rider needs to change direction quickly to the right to avoid debris. Which handgrip do they press?
choices: The right handgrip, to lean and go right
The left handgrip, to counter-balance the motorcycle right
Both handgrips equally, to keep the motorcycle upright
Neither — they lean their body right instead
questions.explanation: The same rule that governs ordinary turns governs a swerve: apply hand pressure to the handgrip located on the side of your intended direction of escape. Press right, lean right, go right — then press the opposite handgrip once clear to return to your original direction of travel.
choiceExplanations: Pressing left leans the motorcycle left, which is the wrong direction for this hazard.
Pressing both equally produces no lean and therefore no change of direction.
Body lean alone is not the manual's swerve technique; hand pressure on the handgrip is.

questions.question: In a slow, tight turn, what should the rider do?
choices: Lean the motorcycle only and keep their body upright
Lean with the motorcycle at the same angle
Lean the body further than the motorcycle
Keep the motorcycle upright and steer with the handlebars alone
questions.explanation: The manual distinguishes two cases: in regular turns the rider and motorcycle lean together at the same angle, and in slow, tight turns you counterbalance by leaning the motorcycle only and keeping your body upright. The rider's upright weight is what keeps a slow, steeply leaned motorcycle from falling in.
choiceExplanations: Leaning together at the same angle is what you do in regular turns, not slow tight ones.
Leaning the body further than the motorcycle is not a technique the manual describes.
The motorcycle must lean to turn; keeping it upright is not an option in a tight turn.

questions.question: Which situation calls for leaning together with the motorcycle at the same angle?
choices: A regular turn at road speed
A slow, tight turn in a car park
A U-turn at walking pace
Manoeuvring the motorcycle at idle
questions.explanation: The manual contrasts the two: in regular turns the rider and the motorcycle should lean together at the same angle, while in slow, tight turns you counterbalance by leaning the motorcycle only and keeping your body upright. Speed is what decides which technique applies.
choiceExplanations: Slow, tight turns call for counterbalancing, with the body kept upright.
A walking-pace U-turn is the counterbalancing case, not the lean-together case.
Manoeuvring at idle is slow, tight work where the rider stays upright.

questions.question: When should gears be changed relative to a turn?
choices: Before entering the turn
At the apex of the turn
As the motorcycle begins to lean
Immediately after the lean angle is greatest
questions.explanation: The manual says it is best to change gears before entering a turn, and that if shifting in the turn is necessary you must do it smoothly, because a sudden change in power to the rear wheel can cause a skid. Gear selection belongs with the SLOW step, not with the lean.
choiceExplanations: The apex is mid-turn, where a sudden power change to the rear wheel can cause a skid.
Changing gear while initiating the lean adds an unsettling input at the worst moment.
Shifting while still leaned over carries the same skid risk the manual warns about.

questions.question: Which action is NOT part of proper firm braking?
choices: Grabbing the front brake lever for maximum initial bite
Keeping your knees against the tank and your eyes up
Squeezing the front brake progressively harder as weight transfers forward
Using light-to-lighter pressure on the rear brake pedal
questions.explanation: The manual warns not to grab the brake lever or use abrupt pressure, because grabbing at the front brake or jamming down on the rear can cause the brakes to lock, resulting in control problems. The other three actions are exactly what the manual prescribes.
choiceExplanations: This is correct technique; it helps you stop in a straight line.
This is correct — more front traction becomes available as weight moves forward.
This is correct — rear traction falls as weight transfers, so rear pressure lightens.

questions.question: Vehicles are being operated on both sides of you. Which lane path is usually your best option?
choices: Path 2, the centre of the lane
Path 1, the left third
Path 3, the right third
Whichever path is closest to the shoulder
questions.explanation: The manual states that if vehicles are being operated on both sides of you, the centre of the lane, path 2, is usually your best option. It keeps a cushion on each side rather than sacrificing one to gain the other.
choiceExplanations: The left third is the choice when hazards are on your right only, not on both sides.
The right third is the choice when problems are on your left only, not on both sides.
Riding at the lane edge gives up the space cushion on the other side entirely.

questions.question: Parked cars line the right side of the road and there is no oncoming traffic. Which path does the manual's rule point to?
choices: Path 1 or 2 — keep away from the hazards on your right
Path 3, closest to the parked cars, so drivers can see you
Path 2 only, regardless of where the hazards are
Alternate between all three paths to stay unpredictable
questions.explanation: The manual says to remain in path 1 or 2 if hazards are on your right only, and to ride in path 2 or 3 if problems are on your left only. It also says that when passing parked cars you should stay toward the left of your lane, which is the same answer arrived at from the other direction.
choiceExplanations: Riding nearest the parked cars puts you where doors open and people step out.
The centre is the answer when hazards are on both sides; here they are on one side only.
Unpredictable lane use is not a strategy the manual offers; position is chosen for a reason.

questions.question: What does the manual say collects in the centre third of the lane?
choices: Debris and oil drippings from cars
Rainwater, because the road crowns toward the centre
Loose gravel thrown from the shoulder
Nothing — the centre is always the cleanest part of the lane
questions.explanation: The manual says the centre third of the lane is the place where debris and oil drippings from cars collect and where hazards such as surface covers are located. It immediately adds the balancing point: unless the road is wet, the typical centre strip permits adequate traction.
choiceExplanations: Road crown drains water toward the edges, and the manual does not identify the centre as a water channel.
Dirt and gravel collect along the sides of the road, especially on curves and ramps.
The manual expressly identifies the centre strip as where debris and oil drippings gather.

questions.question: Which statement about the centre of the lane is NOT correct?
choices: The centre third must always be avoided because of oil and grease
Unless the road is wet, the typical centre strip permits adequate traction
You can ride to the left or right of the grease strip and still be within the centre third
Big buildups of oil and grease at busy intersections and tollbooths should be avoided

choiceExplanations: This is correct — the manual makes this exact qualification about traction.

This is correct — the manual singles out busy intersections and tollbooths for buildups.

questions.question: What is the normal minimum following distance behind another vehicle?
choices: Two seconds
One second
Three seconds
One motorcycle length per 10 mph
questions.explanation: The manual states that normally, a minimum of two seconds distance should be maintained when following a vehicle. Two seconds leaves a minimum amount of space to stop or swerve if the driver ahead stops suddenly, and it also gives you a better view of potholes and other hazards in the road.
choiceExplanations: One second leaves no usable margin to stop or swerve if the driver ahead stops suddenly.
Three seconds or more is the figure for slippery pavement, poor visibility or heavy traffic.
The manual measures following distance in seconds, not in vehicle lengths.

questions.question: How much distance does a motorcycle need to stop compared with a car?
choices: In traffic, as much distance as a car
About half as much, because it is lighter
About a quarter as much, because of the front brake
Twice as much, because it has less braking surface
questions.explanation: The manual states plainly that in traffic, motorcycles need as much distance to stop as cars. That is why the same two-second minimum applies, and why riders who assume a motorcycle stops shorter follow too closely — a frequent factor in crashes involving motorcyclists.
choiceExplanations: The manual does not credit motorcycles with shorter stopping distances in traffic.
The front brake provides 70% or more of stopping power, but that does not halve the distance.
The manual does not say a motorcycle needs more distance than a car in ordinary traffic.

questions.question: Which condition calls for opening up a three-second or more following distance?
choices: Slippery pavement, or traffic heavy enough that someone may squeeze in front of you
Riding on a road you know well
Riding behind a motorcycle rather than a car
Riding in the centre portion of the lane
questions.explanation: The manual lists three triggers for a larger cushion: if the pavement is slippery, if you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, or if traffic is heavy and someone may squeeze in front of you. choiceExplanations: Familiarity with a road is a reason to ride slower at night, not a reason to shorten the gap.
The vehicle type ahead does not change the following distance rule.
Lane position and following distance are separate decisions.

questions.question: You are following a van on a wet road at night. What following distance does the manual point to?

Two seconds, the standard minimum
One second, since the van's brake lights are easy to see
Whatever gap keeps the van's tail lights in view
questions.explanation: Three of the manual's triggers apply at once here: the pavement is slippery, you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, and it is night, when the manual separately says to open up a three-second following distance or more. Each on its own would justify more than two seconds.
choiceExplanations: Two seconds is the normal minimum; this situation stacks three separate reasons to exceed it.
A short gap removes any room to stop, and brake lights do not create stopping distance.
Keeping tail lights in view is not a measure of stopping distance at all.

questions.question: How do you check your following distance using a marker on the road?
choices: Count 'one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two' from when the vehicle ahead passes it
Count the number of dashed lane markings between you and the vehicle ahead
Estimate the gap in motorcycle lengths
Time how long the vehicle ahead takes to reach the marker
questions.explanation: The manual's method is to pick a marker such as a pavement marking or lamppost, and when the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, count off the seconds. If you reach the marker before you reach 'two', you are following too closely.
choiceExplanations: Counting lane markings measures distance, not the time gap the manual uses.
Vehicle lengths are not the measure; the manual counts seconds.
You time yourself reaching the marker after the vehicle ahead, not the vehicle's own approach.

questions.question: You count 'one-thousand-one' and reach the marker. What does that tell you?
choices: You are following too closely and should drop back
You are at a safe two-second distance
You have a three-second cushion
Nothing useful — the count only works above 40 mph
questions.explanation: The rule is that if you reach the marker before you reach 'two', you are following too closely. Arriving on the count of one is about a one-second gap — half the normal minimum — and leaves almost nothing with which to stop or swerve.
choiceExplanations: Reaching the marker at 'one' is roughly a one-second gap, half the stated minimum.
A three-second cushion would mean reaching the marker after the full count of three.
The manual applies the counting method without any speed qualification.

questions.question: What is the manual's recommended way to deal with someone following you too closely?
choices: Get them in front of you — let them pass, or slow and open space ahead
Speed up until they fall back
Brake sharply to warn them off
Move to the edge of the lane and maintain speed
questions.explanation: The manual says a better way to handle tailgaters is to get them in front of you: when someone is following too closely, try to let them pass. If you cannot, slow down and open up extra space ahead to allow room for both you and the tailgater to stop, which also encourages them to pass.
choiceExplanations: The manual warns this can simply produce a tailgater at a higher speed.
Sharp braking in front of a tailgater invites the rear-end collision you are trying to avoid.
Moving to the lane edge does not remove the tailgater and gives up your space cushion.

questions.question: Why does the manual reject speeding up to shake off a tailgater?
choices: It can end up with someone tailgating you at a higher speed
It is illegal to exceed the speed limit to avoid a tailgater
It uses more fuel than slowing down
It makes your brake light harder to see
questions.explanation: The manual's reasoning is that speeding up to lose someone following too closely can end up with someone tailgating you at a higher speed. The problem has not been solved, only made faster. Getting them in front of you removes it entirely.
choiceExplanations: The manual's objection is practical, not a statement about the speed limit.
Fuel use is nowhere part of the manual's reasoning.
Brake light visibility is discussed separately and is not affected by your speed.

questions.question: Where should you ride before beginning a pass?
choices: In the left portion of your lane at a safe following distance
In the right portion of your lane to leave room to pull out
Directly behind the vehicle's bumper for the shortest pass
Alongside the vehicle before signalling
questions.explanation: The manual's first passing step is to ride in the left portion of the lane at a safe following distance to increase your line of sight and make you more visible. You then signal and check for oncoming traffic, using your mirrors and turning your head to check your blind spot.
choiceExplanations: The right portion narrows your line of sight past the vehicle ahead.
Closing right up removes your view ahead and your stopping distance.
Riding alongside before signalling puts you in the blind spot with no plan.

source.sourceQuote: Ride in the left portion of the lane at a safe following distance to increase your line of sight and make you more visible.

questions.question: Which statement about passing does the manual NOT support?
choices: A pass may be completed above the posted limit if it shortens the time alongside
Do not linger in the blind spot
Signal again before returning to your original lane, then cancel the signal
Check your mirrors and turn your head before moving out
questions.explanation: The manual states that passes must be completed within posted speed limits, and only where permitted. Nothing about shortening exposure alongside another vehicle licenses exceeding the limit; the other three statements are steps the manual gives.
choiceExplanations: This is correct — time spent in another driver's blind spot is time they cannot see you.
This is correct — the manual's fourth passing step is exactly this.
This is correct — mirrors plus a headcheck before moving out is the first step.

questions.question: When another vehicle is passing you from behind, where should you ride?
choices: In the centre portion of your lane
In the portion of the lane closest to the passing vehicle
On the shoulder until the pass is complete
As far right as possible, regardless of the passing side
questions.explanation: The manual says that when you are being passed from behind, stay in the centre portion of your lane, because riding close to the passing vehicle could put you in a hazardous situation. The four hazards it names are a sideswipe, extended mirrors, objects thrown from windows, and blasts of wind from larger vehicles.
choiceExplanations: Riding close to the passing vehicle exposes you to extended mirrors, sideswipes and windblast.
Leaving the road surface for a routine pass introduces a loose-surface hazard for no gain.
Hugging one edge gives up your cushion and may put you on debris at the lane edge.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c

questions.question: A large truck is overtaking you on a windy day. What does the manual say about your position?
choices: Being in the farther portion of the lane gives you more room for error when the windblast hits
Move closer to the truck so the blast passes over you
Accelerate to match the truck's speed until it moves ahead
Pull onto the shoulder and stop until it has passed
questions.explanation: The manual lists blasts of wind from larger vehicles among the hazards of being passed, and says you have more room for error if you are in the farther portion when hit by this blast than if you are closer to their lane. Staying in the centre portion of your own lane is the position it recommends.
choiceExplanations: Moving closer increases exposure to the blast, to extended mirrors and to a sideswipe.
Matching speed keeps you alongside in the blind spot for longer, which the manual warns against.
Stopping on the shoulder for a routine overtake creates its own hazard and is not advised.

questions.question: What does the manual say about lane sharing?
choices: Cars and motorcycles need a full lane to operate safely, and lane sharing is usually prohibited
Lane sharing is safe provided both vehicles are moving slowly
Lane sharing is permitted when traffic is stopped
Lane sharing is encouraged in heavy traffic to reduce congestion
questions.explanation: The manual states that cars and motorcycles need a full lane to operate safely, and that lane sharing is usually prohibited. Riding between rows of stopped or moving cars in the same lane leaves you vulnerable to a hand out of a window, a door opening, or a car turning suddenly.
choiceExplanations: Low speed does not remove the hazards: a door could open or a car could turn suddenly.
The manual gives no stopped-traffic exception; it warns specifically about rows of stopped cars.
The manual discourages lane sharing rather than encouraging it.

questions.question: Drivers are most tempted to squeeze past you in the same lane in which situation?
choices: Heavy, bumper-to-bumper traffic
On an open rural road at speed
When you are riding in the left portion of the lane on a motorway
When your headlight is on during the day
questions.explanation: The manual lists the situations where drivers are most tempted to squeeze by: in heavy, bumper-to-bumper traffic, when they want to pass you, when you are preparing to turn at an intersection, and when you are moving into an exit lane or leaving a highway. Keeping a centre-portion position discourages it.
choiceExplanations: Open roads with space to overtake properly are not where drivers try to share a lane.
Lane position can discourage sharing, but the temptation the manual names is heavy traffic.
A daytime headlight increases your conspicuity; it does not invite lane sharing.

questions.question: A driver is coming down an entrance ramp onto the highway ahead of you. What does the manual advise?
choices: Give them plenty of room — change lanes if one is open, or adjust speed to open space
Hold your speed and lane so the merging driver can predict you
Speed up to clear the merge point before they arrive
Move to the lane edge nearest the ramp so they can see you
questions.explanation: The manual says drivers on an entrance ramp may not see you on the highway, so give them plenty of room. Change to another lane if one is open; if there is no room for a lane change, adjust speed to open up space for the merging vehicle.
choiceExplanations: Predictability does not help a driver who has not seen you at all, which is the stated problem.
Racing a merging vehicle to the same point is the opposite of creating a space cushion.
Moving toward the ramp reduces your escape room instead of increasing it.

questions.question: Why does the manual tell you not to ride next to cars or trucks in other lanes?
choices: You may be in a blind spot, and vehicles alongside block your escape from danger ahead
It makes it harder for you to see traffic signals
It increases fuel consumption from wind turbulence
It is prohibited on multi-lane highways
questions.explanation: The manual gives two reasons together: you might be in the blind spot and a vehicle could switch into your lane without warning, and vehicles in the next lane also block your escape if you come upon danger in your own lane. Its advice is to speed up or drop back to find a place clear of traffic on both sides.
choiceExplanations: Signal visibility is not the reason the manual gives for avoiding positions alongside vehicles.
Fuel use is never part of the manual's safety reasoning.
The manual gives a safety reason, not a legal prohibition, for avoiding this position.

questions.question: Why does the manual say to keep well behind the vehicle ahead even when you are stopped?
choices: So you can get out of the way if someone bears down on you from behind
So your headlight does not dazzle the driver ahead
So the engine does not overheat in traffic
Because stopping closer is prohibited at traffic signals
questions.explanation: The manual says keeping well behind the vehicle ahead even when stopped makes it easier to get out of the way if someone bears down on you from behind, and gives you a cushion if the vehicle ahead starts to back up. A stopped motorcycle with no space in front of it has nowhere to go.
choiceExplanations: Dazzle is not the manual's concern here; escape room is.
Engine temperature is not among the reasons the manual gives.
No legal stopping distance at signals is stated in the manual.

questions.question: Where should you ride so the driver ahead can see you in their inside rearview mirror?
choices: The centre portion of the lane
The far left of the lane
The far right of the lane
Directly in the driver's left blind spot
questions.explanation: The manual says that when behind a car, ride where the driver can see you in the inside rearview mirror, and that riding in the centre portion of the lane should put you in view. Riding at the far side of a lane may only put you in a sideview mirror, which most drivers check far less often.
choiceExplanations: The far side of a lane may only show you in a sideview mirror, which drivers check far less often.
The same problem applies on the right: sideview mirrors get much less attention.
A blind spot is by definition where the driver cannot see you at all.

questions.question: What do the three letters of SEE stand for?
choices: Search, Evaluate, Execute
Scan, Estimate, Escape
Slow, Evaluate, Exit
See, Expect, Escape
questions.explanation: The manual describes SEE as the MSF's three-step strategy: Search, Evaluate, Execute. It exists to help you assess what is going on in traffic so you can plan and implement the safest course of action as traffic situations change.
choiceExplanations: Scan and estimate are plausible words, but the manual's three steps are search, evaluate and execute.
SLOW is the first step of a turn, not of the SEE strategy.
The strategy is not a description of expectations; its final step is a physical action.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the SEE strategy?
choices: To assess traffic so you can plan and carry out the safest course of action as situations change
To pass the on-cycle skills test
To keep the motorcycle stable in corners
To decide which lane position is legal
questions.explanation: The manual says SEE will help you assess what is going on in traffic so you can plan and implement the safest course of action as traffic situations change. It is the reasoning layer behind the specific rules, which is why it applies to situations the manual never lists.
choiceExplanations: The skills test measures physical control; SEE is a mental strategy for traffic.
Cornering stability is handled by the four steps of a turn, not by SEE.
Lane position is a tool SEE uses, but legality is not what the strategy decides.

questions.question: When searching, what does the manual tell you to focus on finding?
choices: Potential escape paths
The speed limit signs
Other motorcyclists
Police vehicles
questions.explanation: The manual says that as you search, focus on finding potential escape paths, especially in or around intersections, shopping areas and school and construction zones. An escape path is what converts a surprise into a manoeuvre instead of a collision.
choiceExplanations: Speed limits matter, but the search is about where you could go if something goes wrong.
Other riders are not the object of the search strategy.
Enforcement is irrelevant to the manual's search priorities.

Interstate highways and toll plazas
Rural two-lane roads at night
Residential streets with parked cars
questions.explanation: The manual names intersections, shopping areas, and school and construction zones both as search priorities and, later, as the potential high-risk areas where you should cover the clutch and both brakes to reduce the time you need to react.
choiceExplanations: Highways are not the manual's named high-risk search areas; conflict points are.
Night riding gets its own advice, but these are not the named searching priorities.

questions.question: How far ahead is the manual's long search distance, expressed in time?

About 4 seconds
About 2 seconds
About 30 seconds
questions.explanation: The manual says to search for hazards that are further out, looking ahead to an area it would take about 12 seconds to reach. That distance provides time to prepare for a situation before it becomes urgent, which the shorter lead times cannot do.

Two seconds is the minimum following distance behind the vehicle ahead.
Thirty seconds is not a figure the manual uses.

12 seconds
questions.explanation: The manual states that anything within 4 seconds of your path is considered immediate, because 4 seconds can provide enough time and space to swerve and/or brake for fixed hazards or for someone or something entering your path.

Eight seconds is not one of the manual's three lead times.

1 second

questions.question: A rider keeps a good gap behind the car ahead but never looks beyond it. Which part of the search are they missing?
choices: The 12-second look that lets them prepare before a situation becomes urgent
The 2-second following distance
The mirror check behind them
The lean-angle assessment for the next curve
questions.explanation: The manual's point in giving three lead times is that they do different jobs. A 2-second gap handles the vehicle in front. Only the search to an area about 12 seconds ahead provides time to prepare for a situation before it becomes urgent, and that is exactly what this rider has given up.
choiceExplanations: A good gap behind the car ahead is the 2-second distance, which they already have.

questions.question: What does the Evaluate step ask you to do?
choices: Think about how hazards can interact to create risks for you
Estimate your stopping distance at the current speed
Judge whether other drivers have seen you
Decide whether the road surface is legal to ride on
questions.explanation: The manual defines it directly: evaluate means to think about how hazards can interact to create risks for you. It then tells you to anticipate potential problems and have a plan to reduce risks, considering road and surface characteristics, traffic control devices, other vehicles, and available escape paths.
choiceExplanations: Stopping distance is one input, but Evaluate is about how hazards combine into risk.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the things the manual tells you to evaluate?
choices: The registration status of vehicles around you
Road and surface characteristics such as potholes and guardrails
Traffic control devices including signals, warning signs and pavement markings
Escape paths, in front or to the sides
questions.explanation: The manual's Evaluate list covers road and surface characteristics, traffic control devices, vehicles and other traffic that may move into your path, and escape paths. Nothing about other vehicles' paperwork appears, and nothing in it would help you predict what they do next.
choiceExplanations: This is on the manual's list — surface features shape your riding strategy.
This is on the list — traffic control devices require you to evaluate circumstances ahead.

questions.question: How does the manual say the Execute step should be carried out?
choices: With smoothness and precision
As quickly as possible, whatever it takes
Only after the hazard has clearly committed
By braking first in every case
questions.explanation: The manual says to execute your decision with smoothness and precision. The three actions available are communicating your presence with lights and/or horn, adjusting your speed by accelerating, stopping or slowing, and adjusting your position or direction by swerving, changing lanes, or moving within your lane.
choiceExplanations: Abrupt inputs cause skids; the manual asks for smooth, precise action rather than raw speed.
Waiting for a hazard to commit removes the time and space that make a response possible.
Braking is one of three tools; sometimes the answer is to accelerate or change position.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the three ways the manual says to execute a decision?
choices: Communicating your presence with lights and/or horn
Signalling to other riders with hand signals
Sounding the horn continuously until the hazard clears
Stopping in the traffic lane until the situation resolves
questions.explanation: The manual's Execute actions are: communicating your presence with lights and/or horn, adjusting your speed, and adjusting your position and/or direction. Communicating is first because it can remove the hazard before any evasive action is needed.
choiceExplanations: Hand signals are a group-riding tool, not one of the three Execute actions.
The manual says to sound the horn loud and long in an emergency, but continuous use is not the strategy.
Stopping in a live lane creates a new hazard rather than executing a decision.

questions.question: Two hazards are developing at once. What does the manual advise?
choices: Adjust speed to let them separate, then deal with them one at a time
Deal with the nearer one and accept the risk from the other
Split the difference and pass between them
Brake to a stop until both have cleared
questions.explanation: The manual applies the old adage 'one step at a time' to two or more hazards: adjust speed to permit two hazards to separate, then deal with them one at a time as single hazards. Decision-making becomes more complex with three or more, where you evaluate the consequences of each and give equal distance to the hazards.
choiceExplanations: Ignoring one hazard abandons the evaluation instead of resolving it.
Splitting the difference gives equal exposure to both rather than separating them in time.
Stopping in traffic is not the manual's answer; adjusting speed to separate hazards is.

source.sourceQuote: Apply the old adage “one step at a time” to handle two or more hazards.

questions.question: In potential high-risk areas such as intersections and school zones, what does the manual tell you to cover?
choices: The clutch and both brakes
The horn button only
The clutch only
The rear brake only
questions.explanation: The manual says that in potential high-risk areas, such as intersections, shopping areas, and school and construction zones, cover the clutch and both brakes to reduce the time you need to react. It repeats the same instruction in the intersections section.
choiceExplanations: The horn is one Execute tool, but covering it does not reduce braking reaction time.
Covering the clutch alone leaves the brakes an extra movement away.
The rear brake alone provides under a third of stopping power; both brakes are covered.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - SEE

questions.question: What does the manual call the habit of aggressively scanning ahead, to the sides and behind?
choices: Using your RiderRadar
Running a T-CLOCS sweep
Counterbalancing
A staggered scan
questions.explanation: The manual describes using your 'RiderRadar' to aggressively scan the environment ahead of you, to the sides, and behind you to avoid potential hazards even before they arise. It is the active, searching-out form of looking that the Search step calls for.
choiceExplanations: T-CLOCS is the pre-ride inspection checklist, not a scanning habit.
Counterbalancing is a body-position technique for slow, tight turns.
Staggered formation is a group-riding spacing pattern.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - SEE
source.sourceQuote: aggressively scan the environment ahead of you, to the sides, and behind you to avoid potential hazards even before they arise

questions.question: What proportion of motorcycle/car crashes does the manual attribute to drivers violating a rider's right-of-way?
choices: Over one-half
About one-quarter
About one-tenth
Nearly all of them
questions.explanation: The manual states that over one-half of motorcycle/car crashes are caused by drivers violating a rider's right-of-way. That is why it treats intersections as the greatest potential for conflict between you and other traffic.
choiceExplanations: One-quarter badly understates the figure the manual gives.
One-tenth is far below the manual's figure.
The manual says over one-half, not almost all — riders also contribute to crashes.

source.sourceQuote: Over one-half of motorcycle/car crashes are caused by drivers violating a rider's right-of-way.

questions.question: Which vehicle movement does the manual identify as the biggest danger at intersections?
choices: Cars turning left in front of you
Cars following you too closely through the junction
Cars stopping suddenly ahead of you
Cars overtaking you as you enter the junction
questions.explanation: The manual names cars that turn left in front of you — including cars turning left from the lane on your right — and cars on side streets that pull into your lane as the biggest dangers. The left-turning car across your path is the classic motorcycle crash.
choiceExplanations: Tailgaters are a hazard, but they are not the manual's named intersection danger.
Sudden stops ahead are a following-distance problem, not the intersection danger named here.
Being overtaken has its own guidance and is not the biggest intersection danger.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Cars that turn left in front of you, including cars turning left from the lane on your right, and cars on side streets that pull into your lane, are the biggest dangers.

questions.question: According to the manual, what counts as an intersection?
choices: Anywhere traffic may cross your path of travel, including a residential driveway
Only junctions controlled by a signal or a stop sign
Only the crossing of two or more numbered roads
Only places where lanes of traffic physically merge
questions.explanation: The manual says an intersection can be in the middle of an urban area or at a driveway on a residential street — anywhere traffic may cross your path of travel. A driveway with no markings and no signs is still an intersection for the purpose of the strategy.
choiceExplanations: Control devices do not define an intersection; crossing paths do.
Road classification has nothing to do with the manual's definition.
Merging is a separate situation with its own guidance.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: An intersection can be in the middle of an urban area or at a driveway on a residential street

questions.question: A driver waiting to pull out appears to look directly at you. What does the manual say this means?
choices: Nothing reliable — a driver can look right at a rider and still fail to see them
You have been seen and may proceed at your normal speed
The driver has yielded the right-of-way to you
You should accelerate to clear the junction before they move
questions.explanation: The manual is unambiguous: there are no guarantees that others see you, and you should never count on eye contact, because too often a driver looks right at a motorcyclist and still fails to see him or her. The only eyes you can count on are your own.
choiceExplanations: The manual says there are no guarantees that others see you, so this is not a safe conclusion.
Looking at you is not yielding, and nothing has been communicated.
Accelerating removes your options if the driver does pull out; the manual says to slow and cover the controls.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: There are no guarantees that others see you. Never count on “eye contact.”

questions.question: What assumption does the manual tell you to make about a car that could enter your path?
choices: Assume that it will
Assume it will yield if you have the green
Assume it will see your headlight
Assume it will stop at the line
questions.explanation: The manual's rule is blunt: if a car can enter your path, assume that it will. It adds that good riders are always 'looking for trouble' — not to get into it, but to stay out of it.
choiceExplanations: Having the right-of-way does not stop a driver who violates it — that is most of these crashes.
A daytime headlight helps, but the manual never treats being seen as guaranteed.
Cars on side streets pulling into your lane are one of the two biggest dangers named.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: If a car can enter your path, assume that it will.

questions.question: Approaching an intersection where a driver is preparing to cross your path, what should you cover?
choices: The clutch lever and both brakes
The horn and the front brake
The clutch only
The rear brake only
questions.explanation: The manual says to cover the clutch lever and both brakes to reduce reaction time. Covering the controls removes the time it would otherwise take to find them, which is the difference between stopping short and not.
choiceExplanations: The horn is useful but covering it does nothing for your braking reaction time.
Covering the clutch alone leaves both brakes a hand and foot movement away.
The rear brake supplies under a third of stopping power; both brakes are covered.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Cover the clutch lever and both brakes to reduce reaction time.

questions.question: Which action does the manual recommend when approaching an intersection where a vehicle may cross your path?
choices: Slow and select a lane position that increases your visibility to that driver
Speed up to shorten the time you are exposed
Move as far right as possible to stay out of the way
Hold your speed and position so the driver can judge you accurately
questions.explanation: The manual says that when approaching an intersection where a vehicle driver is preparing to cross your path, slow and select a lane position to increase your visibility to that driver, then cover the clutch lever and both brakes. As you enter, move away from the vehicle.
choiceExplanations: Speeding up reduces the time and space you have if the driver does pull out.
The right edge may hide you behind other traffic and removes your escape path.
Holding position assumes the driver has seen you, which the manual says you cannot assume.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Cover the clutch lever and both brakes to reduce reaction time.

questions.question: Why does the manual warn against changing speed or position radically at an intersection?
choices: Drivers might think you are preparing to turn
It uses up traction you may need for braking
It makes your headlight harder to see
It is prohibited within 100 feet of a junction
questions.explanation: The manual says not to change speed or position radically, as drivers might think you are preparing to turn. Lane position is one of the ways a rider communicates intentions, so a large sudden movement sends a message you did not intend to send.
choiceExplanations: Traction loss is a cornering and braking concern, not the reason given here.
Headlight visibility does not change with speed or lane position adjustments.
No such distance rule appears in the manual.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Do not change speed or position radically, as drivers might think you are preparing to turn.

questions.question: An oncoming vehicle is signalling a left turn in the middle of a block, nowhere near an intersection. What does the manual advise?
choices: Use the same intersection strategy — slow, position for visibility, cover the controls
Ignore it, since the strategy only applies at intersections
Accelerate past before the vehicle can turn
Move to the right edge of your lane and maintain speed
questions.explanation: The manual closes the intersection strategy with this extension: this strategy should also be used whenever a vehicle in the oncoming lane of traffic is signaling for a left turn, whether at an intersection or not. A driveway mid-block produces the same crash as a junction.
choiceExplanations: The manual expressly extends the strategy beyond intersections for exactly this situation.
Accelerating shortens your own reaction time and options if the vehicle turns.
Maintaining speed at the lane edge gives up both visibility and escape room.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Do not change speed or position radically, as drivers might think you are preparing to turn.

questions.question: Approaching a blind intersection, which part of the lane should you move to?
choices: The portion that brings you into the other driver's field of vision earliest
The portion nearest the kerb, to leave room to stop
The centre, regardless of where the obstruction is
The portion closest to the obstruction, to see around it sooner
questions.explanation: The manual says that if you approach a blind intersection, move to the portion of the lane that will bring you into another driver's field of vision at the earliest possible moment. In its own illustration the rider moves to the left portion of the lane — away from the parked car — so the driver on the cross street can see him earlier.
choiceExplanations: Hugging the kerb usually hides you behind the very thing blocking the view.
A fixed centre position ignores which side the sight line is blocked on.
Moving toward the obstruction delays both your view out and the driver's view of you.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: If you approach a blind intersection, move to the portion of the lane that will bring you into another driver's field of vision at the earliest possible moment.

questions.question: You have a stop sign at a blind intersection. What does the manual tell you to do?
choices: Stop at the sign, then edge forward and stop again just short of the cross-traffic lane
Stop once at the sign, then proceed when the way sounds clear
Roll slowly through while looking both ways
Stop past the line so you can see, with your front wheel in the cross lane
questions.explanation: The manual's procedure is two stops: if you have a stop sign or stop line, stop there first, then edge forward and stop again, just short of where the cross-traffic lane meets your lane. From that position lean your body forward and look around buildings, parked cars or bushes.
choiceExplanations: One stop at the sign leaves the view still blocked, which is the whole problem at a blind junction.
Rolling through is not stopping, and the manual asks for two stops here, not none.
The manual expressly says to keep your front wheel out of the cross lane of travel while you look.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: If you have a stop sign or stop line, stop there first. Then edge forward and stop again, just short of where the cross-traffic lane meets your lane.

questions.question: While edging forward to look at a blind intersection, what must stay out of the cross lane?
choices: Your front wheel
Your mirrors
Your rear wheel
Your headlight beam
questions.explanation: The manual says to lean your body forward and look around the obstruction, and then adds: just make sure your front wheel stays out of the cross lane of travel while you're looking. The wheel is the part that would be struck.
choiceExplanations: Mirror overhang is a concern when being passed, not when looking at a blind junction.
The rear wheel is behind you and is not what crosses the line first.
The manual places no restriction on where the headlight beam falls.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Just make sure your front wheel stays out of the cross lane of travel while you're looking.

questions.question: When passing a line of parked cars with no oncoming traffic, where should you ride?
choices: Toward the left of your lane
Toward the right of your lane, close to the parked cars
In the centre of the lane at all times
On the far side of the centre line
questions.explanation: The manual says that when passing parked cars, stay toward the left of your lane, which avoids problems caused by doors opening, drivers getting out of cars or people stepping from between cars. If oncoming traffic is present, it is usually best to remain in the centre-lane position to maximise your space cushion on both sides.
choiceExplanations: Riding close to the parked cars puts you where doors open and people step out between cars.
The centre is the right answer only when oncoming traffic makes a two-sided cushion necessary.
Crossing the centre line into opposing traffic trades one hazard for a worse one.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: When passing parked cars, stay toward the left of your lane.

questions.question: You are passing parked cars and oncoming traffic is now present. What changes?
choices: Move to the centre-lane position to keep a cushion on both sides
Stay left, since the parked cars are the greater hazard
Move right, closest to the parked cars, to increase the gap to oncoming traffic
Stop and wait for the oncoming traffic to clear
questions.explanation: The manual gives the exception directly: if oncoming traffic is present, it is usually best to remain in the centre-lane position to maximise your space cushion on both sides. With hazards on both sides, the centre is the answer — the same logic as path 2 in the lane-position rules.
choiceExplanations: Staying left gives up the cushion on the side where moving traffic now is.
Riding closest to the parked cars re-introduces the door and pedestrian hazard.
Stopping in the lane creates a hazard and is not what the manual advises.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity

questions.question: A car ahead of you pulls a sudden U-turn across the road. What does the manual say about this?
choices: It is dangerous because it can block the whole roadway, leaving you no place to go
It is easily avoided by braking, since U-turns are slow
It is only a hazard on multi-lane roads
It is predictable once the driver's front wheels turn
questions.explanation: The manual says cars making a sudden U-turn are dangerous, because they may cut you off entirely, blocking the whole roadway and leaving you with no place to go. Since you cannot tell what a driver will do, it advises slowing, getting the driver's attention with your horn, and continuing with caution.
choiceExplanations: The manual does not treat a U-turn as easily handled; it names it as a particular danger.
No road-type limitation appears; the hazard is the vehicle blocking the whole roadway.
The manual says you cannot tell what a driver will do, which is why it advises slowing early.

questions.question: How does the manual say to park in a parallel parking space next to a curb?
choices: At an angle with the rear wheel to the curb
Parallel to the curb with the front wheel touching it
At an angle with the front wheel to the curb
Perpendicular to the curb, facing out into the lane
questions.explanation: The manual says that if parking in a parallel parking space next to a curb, position the motorcycle at an angle with the rear wheel to the curb. It adds a caution worth remembering: some cities have ordinances that require motorcycles to park parallel to the curb.
choiceExplanations: Parallel-to-the-curb parking is noted as a local ordinance variation, not the manual's default.
It is the rear wheel that goes to the curb, not the front.
Facing out into the traffic lane is not a parking position the manual describes.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: If parking in a parallel parking space next to a curb, position the motorcycle at an angle with the rear wheel to the curb.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT part of the manual's intersection strategy?
choices: Accelerate through the junction to reduce your exposure time
Ride with your headlight on
Provide a space cushion that gives you an escape path
Move away from the vehicle as you enter the intersection
questions.explanation: Nothing in the manual recommends accelerating through an intersection. Its instruction is the reverse: slow, select a lane position that increases your visibility, cover the clutch and both brakes, and be prepared to brake hard and hold your position if an oncoming vehicle turns in front of you.
choiceExplanations: This is part of the strategy — a daytime headlight makes you twice as likely to be noticed.
This is part of the strategy — an escape path is what an emergency turns on.
This is part of the strategy — the manual says to move away from the vehicle as you enter.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Ride with your headlight on and be in a lane position that provides the best view of oncoming traffic.

questions.question: What do drivers most often say after a crash with a motorcyclist?
choices: That they never saw the motorcycle
That the motorcycle was speeding
That the motorcycle appeared from a blind spot
That the motorcycle's lights were not working
questions.explanation: The manual states that in crashes with motorcyclists, drivers often say that they never saw the motorcycle. A motorcycle's outline is much smaller than a car's from ahead or behind, and it is difficult to see something you are not looking for.
choiceExplanations: Speed is not what the manual reports drivers saying; failure to see the motorcycle at all is.
Blind spots are a real hazard, but the manual's reported explanation is simply not seeing the rider.
Lighting faults are not what drivers report; they report not noticing the motorcycle.

questions.question: Why do drivers pull out in front of motorcyclists thinking they have plenty of time?
choices: Smaller vehicles appear farther away than they actually are
Motorcycles accelerate more slowly than cars from a standstill
Motorcycle headlights are dimmer than car headlights
Motorcycles are usually travelling below the speed limit
questions.explanation: The manual explains that even if a driver does see you, you are not necessarily safe, because smaller vehicles appear farther away than they actually are. It is common for drivers to pull out in front of motorcyclists thinking they have plenty of time — and too often they are wrong.
choiceExplanations: Acceleration is not the manual's explanation; the misjudgement is about distance.
The manual does not attribute the error to headlight brightness.
Nothing in the manual suggests motorcycles are typically slower than the limit.

questions.question: What mindset does the manual suggest a rider adopt about being seen?
choices: Pretend you're invisible
Assume you have been seen once you make eye contact
Assume cars will yield to the smaller vehicle
Rely on your horn to announce your presence
questions.explanation: The manual's strategy is to pretend you're invisible: if you assume other motorists can't see you, you will tend to ride in a hyper-aware mindset and notice more details in your surroundings. It is a thinking tool, not a claim about how visible you actually are.
choiceExplanations: The manual says never to count on eye contact, because drivers look at riders without seeing them.
Nothing in the manual suggests other traffic will defer to a motorcycle.
A motorcycle's horn is not as loud as a car's, so it cannot be relied on.

questions.question: Bright-coloured riding clothing is most important at what time?
choices: During the day, because most crashes occur in daylight hours
At night, because bright colours reflect headlights
At dawn and dusk only
Only in rain or fog
questions.explanation: The manual states that most crashes occur during daylight hours, and to wear bright-coloured clothing to increase your chances of being seen. Reflective material is treated separately as the night measure; bright colour is the daylight measure.
choiceExplanations: Reflective material is the night tool; bright colour works by daylight.
The manual ties bright colour to daylight generally, not to the transition hours alone.
Poor weather is not the condition the manual attaches bright clothing to.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Most crashes occur during daylight hours. Wear bright-colored clothing to increase your chances of being seen.

questions.question: Which colours does the manual name as your best bets for being seen?
choices: Bright orange, red, yellow or green
Black, grey or navy
Brown or olive
White only
questions.explanation: The manual names bright orange, red, yellow or green jackets and vests as your best bets for being seen, and adds that any bright colour is better than drab or dark colours. Reflective, bright-coloured clothing is best of all.
choiceExplanations: Dark colours are exactly what the manual calls drab, and any bright colour beats them.
Earth tones blend into the roadside rather than standing out from it.
White is not singled out; the manual names four bright colours.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c

source.sourceQuote: Bright orange, red, yellow or green jackets/vests are your best bets for being seen.

questions.question: When should a motorcycle's headlight be on?
choices: At all times
Only from dusk to dawn
Only in rain or fog
Only on roads over 45 mph
questions.explanation: The manual says a good way to help others see your motorcycle is to have the headlight on at all times, and backs it with a figure: during the day, a motorcycle with its light on is twice as likely to be noticed.
choiceExplanations: Restricting the headlight to darkness gives up its biggest benefit, which is daytime conspicuity.
Weather is one reason for low beam, but the headlight is on regardless of weather.
The manual attaches no speed or road type to the headlight rule.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c

questions.question: Which beam does the manual say to use at night and in fog?
choices: Low beam
High beam
Whichever is brighter
Hazard flashers instead of a beam
questions.explanation: The manual says to use low beam at night and in fog. The high beam has its own rule elsewhere: use it whenever you are not following or meeting a car, to get all the light you can.
choiceExplanations: The high beam is for when you are not following or meeting a car; fog reflects it back at you.
Brightness is not the criterion; the manual names low beam for these two conditions.
Hazard flashers are not a substitute for a headlight.
