source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Use low beam at night and in fog.

questions.question: When does the manual say to use your turn signals?
choices: Any time you plan to change lanes or turn, even when you think no one is around
Only when another vehicle is close enough to be affected
Only when your intention would not otherwise be obvious
Only on multi-lane roads
questions.explanation: The manual says to use your signals any time you plan to change lanes or turn, and to use them even when you think no one else is around. The signal light itself makes you easier to spot, which is why it is worth using even where your intention seems obvious.
choiceExplanations: The manual explicitly includes the case where you think no one else is around.
The manual says to signal even when what you plan to do is obvious, because the light makes you visible.
Road type does not change the signalling rule.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Use them anytime you plan to change lanes or turn. Use them even when you think no one else is around.

questions.question: You complete a turn and your signal keeps blinking. What risk does the manual identify?
choices: A driver may pull directly into your path, thinking you plan to turn again
The battery may drain and the headlight dim
It is a citable equipment offence
The blinking distracts you from your mirrors
questions.explanation: The manual warns that once you turn, you must make sure your signal is off, or a driver may pull directly into your path, thinking you plan to turn again. An uncancelled signal is a false message, and drivers act on it.
choiceExplanations: Battery drain is not a concern the manual raises about signals.
The manual frames this as a crash risk, not an equipment violation.
The concern is what other drivers conclude, not rider distraction.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Once you turn, make sure your signal is off or a driver may pull directly into your path, thinking you plan to turn again.

questions.question: Why does the manual tell riders to flash their brake light before slowing in certain situations?
choices: A motorcycle's brake light is usually not as noticeable as a car's
A flashing brake light is legally required before any turn
It is the only way to signal a lane change
It prevents the brake light bulb from failing
questions.explanation: The manual's reason is visibility: your motorcycle's brake light is usually not as noticeable as the brake lights on a car, so help others notice you by flashing it before you slow. It names the cases — slowing more quickly than expected, slowing where others do not expect it, and stopped at an intersection with traffic approaching from behind.
choiceExplanations: The manual gives no legal requirement to flash the brake light.
Lane changes are signalled with turn signals, mirrors and head checks.
Bulb life is never part of the manual's reasoning.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Your motorcycle's brake light is usually not as noticeable as the brake lights on a car.

questions.question: You are about to turn off a high-speed highway and someone is following closely. What does the manual suggest?
choices: Flash your brake light before you slow
Slow gradually without touching the brakes so the tailgater is not surprised
Speed up through the turn to keep the gap
Move onto the shoulder before braking
questions.explanation: The manual names this exact case: flash your brake light before you slow more quickly than others might expect, such as turning off a high-speed highway, and again if you are being followed closely, because the tailgater may be watching you and not see what is making you slow.
choiceExplanations: Slowing without a brake light gives the follower no warning at all, which is the opposite of the advice.
Carrying extra speed into a turn off a highway is the running-wide error the manual warns about.
Braking on the shoulder introduces a loose-surface hazard for no benefit.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Your motorcycle's brake light is usually not as noticeable as the brake lights on a car.

questions.question: Most motorcycles have rounded convex mirrors. What is their drawback?
choices: They make cars seem farther away than they actually are
They show a narrower view than flat mirrors
They vibrate more than flat mirrors at speed
They cannot be adjusted once fitted
questions.explanation: The manual says most motorcycles have rounded convex mirrors, which provide a wider view of the road behind than flat mirrors do, but they also make cars seem farther away than they actually are. Its advice is to practise with them until you judge distance well, and even then allow extra distance before changing lanes.
choiceExplanations: Convex mirrors give a wider view than flat mirrors, not a narrower one.
Vibration is not a difference the manual draws between mirror types.
Mirrors are adjusted as part of the pre-ride check.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Most motorcycles have rounded (convex) mirrors.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the times the manual says to make a special point of using your mirrors?
choices: While leaned over in a curve
When you are stopped at an intersection
Before you change lanes
Before you slow down
questions.explanation: The manual names three times to make a special point of using your mirrors: when stopped at an intersection, before changing lanes, and before slowing down. Mid-corner is when your eyes belong through the turn, not behind you.
choiceExplanations: This is one of the three named times — watch for cars coming up from behind.
This is one of the three — make sure no one is about to pass you.
This is one of the three — the driver behind may not expect you to slow.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: When you are stopped at an intersection. Watch cars coming up from behind.

questions.question: Why is checking your mirrors not enough before changing lanes?
choices: Motorcycles have blind spots, so you must turn your head and look
Mirrors are illegal to rely on for a lane change
Convex mirrors show only the lane directly behind you
Mirrors vibrate too much to be read at speed
questions.explanation: The manual says checking your mirrors is not enough, because motorcycles have blind spots like cars. Before you change lanes, turn your head and look to the side for other vehicles, and on a road with several lanes check the far lane as well as the one next to you.
choiceExplanations: The manual makes no legal claim about mirrors; the point is that they have blind spots.
Convex mirrors give a wider view than flat mirrors; the problem is blind spots, not width.
Vibration is not the reason the manual gives for head checks.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Checking your mirrors is not enough. Motorcycles have “blind spots” like cars.

questions.question: On a road with several lanes, which lanes should a head check cover?
choices: The far lane as well as the one next to you
Only the lane immediately next to you
Only the lane you are leaving
Only the oncoming lanes
questions.explanation: The manual says that on a road with several lanes, check the far lane and the one next to you, because a driver in the distant lane may head for the same space you plan to take. Frequent head checks should be part of your normal scanning routine.
choiceExplanations: A driver in the distant lane may be heading for the same space you plan to take.
The lane you are leaving is the one you can already see; the risk is in the lane you are entering.
Oncoming traffic matters when passing, but a head check for a lane change covers your own direction.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Before you change lanes, turn your head, and look to the side for other vehicles.

questions.question: When does the manual suggest giving a quick beep of the horn?
choices: Before passing anyone who may move into your lane
Every time you approach an intersection
Whenever a vehicle is following too closely
Whenever you change lanes
questions.explanation: The manual says it is a good idea to give a quick beep before passing anyone that may move into your lane, and lists examples: a driver following the vehicle ahead too closely who may want to pass, a parked car with someone in the driver's seat, and someone in the street riding a bicycle or walking.
choiceExplanations: The horn is not part of the routine intersection strategy, which is about slowing and covering controls.
The answer to a tailgater is to get them in front of you, not to sound the horn.
Lane changes are communicated with signals, mirrors and head checks.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: It is a good idea to give a quick beep before passing anyone that may move into your lane.

questions.question: What does the manual say about relying on your horn in an emergency?
choices: Sound it loud and long, but do not rely on it — a motorcycle's horn is not as loud as a car's
It is the most effective emergency tool a rider has
It should not be used in an emergency because it startles drivers
It should be used instead of braking or swerving
questions.explanation: The manual says that in an emergency you should sound your horn loud and long and be ready to stop or swerve away from the danger — but keep in mind that a motorcycle's horn is not as loud as a car's, so use it but do not rely on it. Time and space to manoeuvre remain the primary tools.
choiceExplanations: The manual explicitly says not to rely on it, because it is quieter than a car's horn.
The manual tells you to use the horn in an emergency, not to avoid it.
The horn supplements braking and swerving; it never replaces them.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Keep in mind that a motorcycle's horn isn't as loud as a car's

questions.question: What following distance does the manual recommend at night?
choices: Three seconds or more
Two seconds, as in daylight
One second, since traffic is lighter
Whatever keeps the vehicle's tail lights in view
questions.explanation: The manual says that at night, distances are harder to judge because your eyes rely on shadows and light contrasts, so open up a three-second following distance or more, and allow more distance to pass and be passed.
choiceExplanations: Two seconds is the daytime minimum; distances are harder to judge at night.
A one-second gap leaves no room to stop, and lighter traffic does not shorten stopping distance.
Tail light visibility is not a measure of stopping distance.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Open up a three-second following distance or more.

questions.question: What does the manual mean by 'do not override your headlight'?
choices: Do not let your total stopping distance exceed the distance your beam illuminates
Do not fit a brighter bulb than the manufacturer specifies
Do not use high beam when following another vehicle
Do not switch the headlight off to save the battery
questions.explanation: The manual defines it precisely: do not override your headlight means do not let your total stopping distance exceed the distance your light beam illuminates — slow down so you can stop within the distance you can see. Riding faster than your lights is riding into a space you have not checked.
choiceExplanations: Bulb wattage is not what the phrase refers to.
High beam use when following is a separate rule, correct in itself but not this one.
The headlight stays on at all times, but that is not what overriding means.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Intersections and Conspicuity
source.sourceQuote: Do not let your total stopping distance exceed the distance your light beam illuminates.

questions.question: Which two skills does the manual call critical in avoiding a crash?
choices: Stopping and swerving
Accelerating and downshifting
Counterbalancing and countersteering
Signalling and head checking
questions.explanation: The manual says to know when and how to stop or swerve, two skills critical in avoiding a crash. It stresses that determining which skill the situation needs is important as well, since it is not always desirable or possible to stop quickly to avoid an obstacle.
choiceExplanations: Acceleration and gear selection are control skills, not the two named crash-avoidance skills.
These are cornering techniques, useful but not the pair the manual names here.
Signals and head checks are communication and searching, not crash avoidance.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Know when and how to stop or swerve, two skills critical in avoiding a crash.

questions.question: Studies show that most crash-involved riders make which braking error?
choices: They underbrake the front tire and overbrake the rear
They underbrake the rear tire and overbrake the front
They use engine braking instead of the brakes
They brake too early and lose road position
questions.explanation: The manual reports that studies show most crash-involved riders underbrake the front tire and overbrake the rear. Since the front brake provides 70% or more of the total stopping power, that pattern wastes most of the braking available and risks a rear-wheel skid at the same time.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the finding — riders under-use the front, which supplies most of the stopping power.
Engine braking is not identified as the crash-involved riders' error.
Braking early is not the error; the error is which brake gets the pressure.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Underbrake the front tire and overbrake the rear.

questions.question: Besides braking errors, what else do studies say crash-involved riders failed to do?
choices: Separate braking from swerving, or choose swerving when it was appropriate
Check their mirrors before the hazard appeared
Downshift before the hazard appeared
Use their horn before the hazard appeared
questions.explanation: The manual's second finding is that crash-involved riders did not separate braking from swerving, or did not choose swerving when it was appropriate. Both halves matter: mixing the two skills, and picking the wrong one.
choiceExplanations: Mirror use is part of searching, not the specific finding the manual reports here.
Gear selection is not named among the crash-involved riders' failures.
Horn use is not what the studies the manual cites identified.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Did not separate braking from swerving or did not choose swerving when it was appropriate.

questions.question: During a quick stop, how should the two brake controls be used?
choices: Both applied at the same time
The rear first, with the front added only once the motorcycle has settled
The front alone, with the rear left untouched
Neither — close the throttle and let engine braking do the work
questions.explanation: The manual says that to stop quickly, apply both brakes at the same time. Do not be shy about using the front brake, but do not grab it — squeeze the lever firmly and progressively while pressing down on the rear.
choiceExplanations: Staging the rear before the front wastes distance and encourages rear-wheel lockup.
Front-only braking gives up the rear brake's contribution to the stop.
Engine braking is far weaker than the brakes and cannot produce a quick stop.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: To stop quickly, apply both brakes at the same time.

questions.question: Your front wheel locks during a hard stop. What must you do?
choices: Release the front brake lever immediately, then reapply with less pressure
Hold the brake on until the motorcycle stops
Increase rear brake pressure to compensate
Release both brakes and coast to a stop
questions.explanation: The manual says that if the front wheel locks, release the front brake lever immediately and reapply with less pressure. Front-wheel skids result in immediate loss of steering control and balance, and failure to fully release the brake lever immediately will result in a crash.
choiceExplanations: Holding a locked front wheel means immediate loss of steering and balance, and a crash.
More rear brake adds a second skid without restoring front traction or steering.
Releasing both brakes throws away the stopping distance you need.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: If the front wheel locks, release the front brake lever immediately, and reapply with less pressure.

questions.question: What does the manual say results from failing to fully release a locked front brake immediately?
choices: A crash
A longer but still controlled stop
A rear-wheel skid
A high-side crash
questions.explanation: The manual states flatly that failure to fully release the brake lever immediately will result in a crash. Front-wheel skids take away steering control and balance at once, and there is no recovery that keeps the brake applied.
choiceExplanations: There is no controlled outcome; the manual says steering and balance are lost immediately.
The rear wheel is a separate case, with its own rules about staying locked.
A high-side comes from releasing a misaligned locked rear wheel, not from a front-wheel skid.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Failure to fully release the brake lever immediately will result in a crash.

questions.question: What causes rear-wheel lockup?
choices: Too much rear brake pressure
Too much front brake pressure
Releasing the clutch too quickly on an upshift
Riding with too little air in the rear tire
questions.explanation: The manual states that too much rear brake pressure causes rear-wheel lockup, and that as soon as the rear wheel locks, your ability to change direction is lost. This is why rear brake pressure gets lighter as weight transfers forward during a stop.
choiceExplanations: Excess front brake pressure locks the front wheel, a different and more urgent problem.
A harsh clutch release can cause a skid on a downshift, but lockup here is a braking problem.
Low tire pressure is associated with wobble, not with rear-wheel lockup under braking.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Too much rear brake pressure causes rear-wheel lockup.

questions.question: You accidentally lock the rear brake on a good traction surface while upright and travelling straight. What does the manual say?
choices: You can keep it locked until you have completely stopped
Release it at once, as you would a locked front wheel
Pump the rear brake to restore traction
Release the rear brake and apply more front brake
questions.explanation: The manual makes a deliberate distinction. If you accidentally lock the rear brake on a good traction surface, you can keep it locked until you have completely stopped — even with a locked rear wheel you can control the motorcycle if it is upright and going in a straight line. The front wheel gets released immediately; the rear, in these conditions, does not.
choiceExplanations: The front-wheel rule does not transfer: releasing a misaligned locked rear can cause a high-side.
Pumping is not a technique the manual gives for a locked rear wheel.
Swapping brakes mid-skid adds a front-wheel lock risk to an already unstable situation.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: If you accidentally lock the rear brake on a good traction surface, you can keep it locked until you have completely stopped

questions.question: What is the danger in releasing a locked rear wheel that is out of alignment with the front?
choices: The motorcycle can snap upright and throw the rider into the air ahead of it
The rear tire will deflate from the flat spot
The front wheel will lock in sympathy
The engine will stall and remove engine braking
questions.explanation: The manual describes the high-side crash: if the rear wheel is out of alignment with the front, releasing it risks the motorcycle abruptly snapping upright and throwing the rider into the air ahead of the motorcycle's path. It adds that even slight misalignment can produce this.
choiceExplanations: Tire damage is a consequence of a skid but not the danger the manual identifies here.
Front and rear brakes lock independently unless the motorcycle has a linked system.
A stall is not what the manual warns about in a high-side.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: The motorcycle can abruptly snap upright, throwing the rider into the air ahead of the motorcycle's path.

questions.question: How much rear-wheel misalignment does the manual say it takes to risk a high-side crash?
choices: Even slight misalignment
At least a 45-degree angle
Enough for the rear tire to leave the lane
Only a full sideways slide
questions.explanation: The manual says that even slight misalignment can result in a high-side crash. That is why the rule about keeping a locked rear wheel locked is conditioned on the motorcycle being upright and going in a straight line.
choiceExplanations: No angle threshold is given, and the manual's warning is far more sensitive than 45 degrees.
Leaving the lane is not the threshold; the wheels only need to be out of line with each other.
A full slide is one case, but the manual warns that even slight misalignment suffices.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: The motorcycle can abruptly snap upright, throwing the rider into the air ahead of the motorcycle's path.

questions.question: You must stop quickly while in a curve and conditions allow it. What comes first?
choices: Straighten and square the handlebars
Apply maximum brake pressure
Downshift to the lowest usable gear
Move to the outside of the lane
questions.explanation: The manual says that if you must stop quickly while in a curve, first straighten and square the handlebars, then stop. Standing the motorcycle up returns the traction that cornering was consuming, which is what makes full braking possible.
choiceExplanations: Maximum braking at lean angle exceeds the traction the leaned tires have available.
Aggressive downshifting adds a rear-wheel skid risk without restoring braking traction.
Lane position does not change the traction problem that lean angle creates.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: If you must stop quickly while in a curve, first straighten and square the handlebars, then stop.

questions.question: You cannot straighten first — you are in a left-hand curve with a danger of running off the road. What does the manual advise?
choices: Brake smoothly and gradually, reducing lean and increasing pressure as traction returns
Apply full brake pressure immediately and accept the lean angle
Release the brakes entirely and ride it out
Swerve into the opposing lane to straighten the line
questions.explanation: The manual names this exact case. If you cannot straighten first — a danger of running off the road in a left-hand curve, or facing oncoming traffic in a right-hand curve — apply the brakes smoothly and gradually. As you slow you can reduce lean angle and apply more brake pressure, and you always straighten the handlebars in the last few feet of stopping.
choiceExplanations: Full pressure at lean angle is exactly what the reduced traction cannot support.
Giving up braking altogether does nothing about the hazard you are stopping for.
Crossing into opposing traffic replaces a braking problem with a head-on risk.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Always straighten the handlebars in the last few feet of stopping to maintain your balance and remain upright.

questions.question: How does the manual define a swerve?
choices: A sudden change in direction
A controlled slide of the rear wheel
A full-lock turn at low speed
A hard stop followed by a turn
questions.explanation: The manual defines a swerve as a sudden change in direction. It is the alternative to stopping when there is not enough room to stop, and deciding which of the two a situation calls for is itself a crash-avoidance skill.
choiceExplanations: A sliding rear wheel is a skid, which the manual treats as a loss of control.
A full-lock turn is a slow-speed manoeuvre, not an evasive change of direction.
The manual insists braking and swerving be separated, not combined into one move.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: A swerve is a sudden change in direction.

questions.question: To swerve to the right around an obstacle, what do you do?
choices: Press the right handgrip so the motorcycle leans right
Press the left handgrip so the motorcycle leans right
Shift your body weight sharply to the right
Turn the handlebars quickly to the right
questions.explanation: The manual says to apply a small amount of hand pressure to the handgrip located on the side of your intended direction of escape, which causes the motorcycle to lean quickly. The sharper the turn needed, the more the motorcycle must lean — and you press the opposite handgrip once clear to return to your original direction.
choiceExplanations: Pressing the left handgrip leans the motorcycle left, taking you into the obstacle, not around it.
The manual says to keep your body upright and let the motorcycle lean underneath you.
The instruction is a press on the handgrip, not a quick turn of the handlebars.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Apply a small amount of hand pressure to the handlegrip located on the side of your intended direction of escape.

questions.question: What should your body do during a swerve?
choices: Stay upright while the motorcycle leans underneath you
Lean further than the motorcycle to help it turn
Lean with the motorcycle at the same angle
Rise off the seat to shift weight forward
questions.explanation: The manual says to keep your body upright and allow the motorcycle to lean in the direction of the turn while keeping your knees against the tank and your feet solidly on the footrests. Let the motorcycle move underneath you, and make your escape path the target of your vision.
choiceExplanations: Leaning further than the motorcycle is not a technique the manual describes for swerving.
Leaning together at the same angle is for regular turns, not for a sudden evasive change.
Rising off the seat is the technique for crossing an obstacle, not for swerving around one.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Keep your body upright and allow the motorcycle to lean in the direction of the turn

questions.question: When should you brake in relation to an aggressive swerve?
choices: Before or after the swerve, never during it
Throughout the swerve, to shed as much speed as possible
Only at the start of the swerve
Only at the mid-point of the swerve
questions.explanation: The manual says that if the situation allows, separate braking from swerving: brake before or after, never while making an aggressive swerve. Traction is finite, and a tire spent on cornering has nothing left for stopping.
choiceExplanations: Braking during the swerve spends the traction the swerve needs to change direction.
The start of the swerve is inside the swerve, which is exactly what the manual rules out.
The mid-point is when lean angle is greatest and the least traction is available for braking.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Did not separate braking from swerving or did not choose swerving when it was appropriate.

questions.question: A car stops suddenly ahead and there is not enough room to stop, but there is a clear gap to your left. What does the manual's guidance point to?
choices: Swerve into the gap, then brake once you are straight and upright
Brake as hard as possible and swerve at the same time
Brake only, and accept the impact if it comes
Swerve while trailing the rear brake to stay settled
questions.explanation: The manual anticipates this: sometimes you may not have enough room to stop even if you use both brakes properly, and the only way to avoid a crash may be to turn quickly or swerve around the obstacle. It then adds the sequencing rule — brake before or after the swerve, never during it.
choiceExplanations: Braking and swerving together is the exact combination the manual tells riders to avoid.
The manual says riders must be able to swerve when stopping will not work, which is this case.
Trailing a brake through the swerve is still braking during the swerve.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: A swerve is a sudden change in direction.

questions.question: What does the manual identify as a primary cause of single-vehicle motorcycle crashes?
choices: Running wide in a curve or turn
Mechanical failure of the front brake
Tire failure at speed
Riding at night without reflective clothing
questions.explanation: The manual states that a primary cause of single-vehicle crashes is motorcyclists running wide in a curve or turn. Its remedy is to be alert to the kind of curve you are entering and to ride within your skill level and the posted speed limits.
choiceExplanations: Brake failure is not identified as a primary cause of single-vehicle crashes.
Tire failure is covered under mechanical problems and is described as rare with maintenance.
Night conspicuity affects crashes with other vehicles, not single-vehicle crashes.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: A primary cause of single-vehicle crashes is motorcyclists running wide in a curve or turn.

questions.question: What lane position does the manual suggest before entering a curve?
choices: Move to the centre of your lane and stay there until you exit
Move to the outside of the lane to straighten the line
Move to the inside of the lane to shorten the corner
Cross to the centre line for maximum sight distance
questions.explanation: The manual says a good choice is to move to the centre of your lane before entering a curve and stay there until you exit. That permits you to spot approaching traffic as soon as possible and to adjust for traffic crowding the centre line or debris blocking part of your lane.
choiceExplanations: Outside entry is advice given for three-wheel motorcycles, not for two-wheel riders here.
Cutting to the inside reduces your sight distance and your margin if the curve tightens.
Riding on the centre line puts you where oncoming traffic crowds and debris collects.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: A good choice is to move to the center of your lane before entering a curve - and stay there until you exit.

questions.question: What does the manual say to be alert to about the shape of a curve?
choices: Whether it stays constant, gradually widens, gets tighter or involves multiple turns
Whether it is banked toward the inside or the outside
Whether it has a posted advisory speed
Whether it is longer or shorter than 100 metres
questions.explanation: The manual says every curve is different and to be alert to whether a curve remains constant, gradually widens, gets tighter or involves multiple turns. A curve that tightens is the one that catches riders out, because the entry speed that felt right no longer is.
choiceExplanations: Camber is not the characteristic the manual asks you to read before a curve.
Posted limits matter, but the manual's list concerns the curve's shape, not its signage.
No curve-length measure appears in the manual.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Be alert to whether a curve remains constant, gradually widens, gets tighter or involves multiple turns.

questions.question: Which statement about quick stops is NOT correct?
choices: Grab the front brake lever hard to use all the available traction at once
Apply both brakes at the same time
Squeeze the front brake lever firmly and progressively
Press down on the rear brake at the same time as the front
questions.explanation: The manual says not to be shy about using the front brake, but not to grab it either — squeeze the brake lever firmly and progressively. Grabbing the front brake locks the wheel, and a locked front wheel means immediate loss of steering control and balance.
choiceExplanations: This is correct — both brakes together is the manual's instruction for a quick stop.
This is correct — squeeze firmly and progressively, never grab.
This is correct — the rear is pressed at the same time, with lighter pressure as weight moves forward.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: To stop quickly, apply both brakes at the same time.

questions.question: If you must ride over a smaller obstacle, at what angle should you approach it?
choices: As close to a 90 degree angle as possible
At about 45 degrees
At the shallowest angle you can manage
Straight along the obstacle's length
questions.explanation: The manual says to try to avoid obstacles by slowing or going around them, but if you must go over a smaller obstacle, approach it at as close to a 90 degree angle as possible. Square-on contact is what stops the front wheel being deflected.
choiceExplanations: Forty-five degrees is the rule for crossing seams and tracks that run parallel to your path.
A shallow angle lets the obstacle deflect the front wheel sideways.
Riding along an obstacle rather than across it keeps the wheel in contact with it.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: If you must go over a smaller obstacle, approach it at as close to a 90˚ angle as possible.

questions.question: What should you do with your body as you ride over an obstacle?
choices: Rise slightly off the seat with your weight on the footrests
Sit down hard to keep the wheels loaded
Lean back and lift the front wheel
Stand fully upright on the footrests
questions.explanation: The manual says to rise slightly off the seat with your weight on the footrests to absorb the shock with your knees and elbows. The full sequence is: slow as much as possible before contact, make sure the motorcycle is straight, rise slightly, and just before contact roll on the throttle slightly to lighten the front end, then roll off.
choiceExplanations: Sitting heavily sends the shock straight through the seat into your spine.
Deliberately lifting the front wheel is not a technique the manual teaches.
Rising slightly is what the manual says; standing fully removes your control position.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Rise slightly off the seat with your weight on the footrests to absorb the shock with your knees and elbows.

questions.question: You have just ridden over an object in the road. What does the manual say to do next?
choices: Pull off the road and check your tires and rims for damage before riding farther
Continue and check at the end of the journey
Brake hard immediately to test the wheels
Ride slowly and listen for unusual noises
questions.explanation: The manual says that if you ride over an object on the street, pull off the road and check your tires and rims for damage before riding any farther. A damaged rim or a cut tire becomes a tire failure at speed later on.
choiceExplanations: Damage found at the end of the journey has already had the whole journey to fail.
Hard braking on a possibly damaged wheel or tire is the opposite of a careful check.
Listening is not a substitute for looking at the tires and rims.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: If you ride over an object on the street, pull off the road and check your tires and rims for damage before riding any farther.

questions.question: When is wet pavement most slippery?
choices: Just after it starts to rain, before surface oil washes to the side of the road
After several hours of heavy rain
Once the rain stops and the surface begins to dry
Only where the road has been recently resurfaced
questions.explanation: The manual lists wet pavement, particularly just after it starts to rain and before surface oil washes to the side of the road, as a poor-traction surface. The oil film lifted by the first water is what makes the opening minutes of a shower the most treacherous.
choiceExplanations: Prolonged rain washes surface oil away, which is why the first minutes are worse.
A drying surface is regaining traction, not losing it.
Resurfacing is not identified as a wet-traction factor in the manual.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Wet pavement, particularly just after it starts to rain and before surface oil washes to the side of the road.

questions.question: Which of these does the manual NOT list as a surface that provides poor traction?
choices: Fresh, dry asphalt on a warm day
Lane markings, steel plates and surface covers, especially when wet
Gravel roads, or places where sand and gravel collect
Mud, leaves, snow and ice
questions.explanation: The manual's poor-traction list is wet pavement just after rain begins, gravel roads or places where sand and gravel collect, mud, leaves, snow and ice, and lane markings, steel plates and surface covers, especially when wet. Dry asphalt is the reference surface, not a hazard.
choiceExplanations: This is on the list — painted and metal surfaces lose grip badly when wet.
This is on the list, and the manual adds that gravel collects on curves and ramps.
This is on the list exactly as written.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Wet pavement, particularly just after it starts to rain and before surface oil washes to the side of the road.

questions.question: What does the manual say about the front brake on a slippery surface?
choices: It is still effective — squeeze the lever gradually to avoid locking the front wheel
It should not be used at all on a slippery surface
It should be used alone, since the rear will lock immediately
It becomes more powerful because less weight transfers forward
questions.explanation: The manual says to use both brakes and that the front brake is still effective, even on a slippery surface — squeeze the brake lever gradually to avoid locking the front wheel. Its summary is gentle pressure on the brakes, not no front brake.
choiceExplanations: Abandoning the front brake gives up most of the stopping power precisely when you need it.
The manual says to use both brakes; the rear is not abandoned either.
Less traction is available, not more; the technique is gradual pressure, not extra force.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: The front brake is still effective, even on a slippery surface.

questions.question: When should you reduce speed for a slippery patch you can see ahead?
choices: Before you reach it
As you cross it
As you leave it
Only if the motorcycle starts to slide
questions.explanation: The manual says to slow down before you get to a slippery surface to lessen your chances of skidding, and adds that it is particularly important to reduce speed before entering wet curves. Once you are on the surface, any sudden change in speed or direction can cause a skid.
choiceExplanations: Braking on the slippery surface is what produces the skid you are trying to avoid.
Slowing after the hazard does nothing about crossing it.
Waiting for a slide means correcting a skid rather than preventing one.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Slow down before you get to a slippery surface to lessen your chances of skidding.

questions.question: Rain has just started falling. Which part of the lane does the manual point you toward?
choices: The tire tracks left by the vehicles ahead
The centre strip between the tire tracks
The painted lane line, which sheds water quickly
The extreme edge of the lane nearest the kerb
questions.explanation: The manual says the centre of a lane can be hazardous when wet, and that when it starts to rain you should ride in the tire tracks left by vehicles. It adds that the left tire track will often be the best position, depending on traffic and other roadway conditions.
choiceExplanations: The centre of a lane can be hazardous when wet, because oil and grease collect there.
Painted lane markings are on the manual's poor-traction list, especially when wet.
Dirt and gravel collect along the sides of the road, which is worse, not better.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: When it starts to rain, ride in the tire tracks left by vehicles.

questions.question: Why does the manual tell you to watch for oil spots when you put a foot down to stop?
choices: You may slip and fall
Oil damages boot soles
Oil spots indicate a leaking motorcycle ahead
Oil marks where the road surface is breaking up
questions.explanation: The manual's warning is simple and physical: watch for oil spots when you put your foot down to stop, because you may slip and fall. The oil that makes the centre strip slippery is the same oil under your boot at a junction.
choiceExplanations: Damage to footwear is not a concern the manual raises.
The manual is describing where oil collects on the road, not diagnosing another vehicle.
Oil pooling is not presented as a sign of surface failure.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: When it starts to rain, ride in the tire tracks left by vehicles.

questions.question: Where do patches of ice tend to develop?
choices: In low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses
On south-facing slopes that catch the sun
On freshly gritted main roads
Only where standing water has pooled
questions.explanation: The manual says rain dries and snow melts faster on some sections of a road than on others, and that patches of ice tend to develop in low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses. It adds that wet surfaces or wet leaves are just as slippery.
choiceExplanations: Sunlit surfaces are where rain dries and snow melts faster, not where ice persists.
Treated main roads are not identified as a place where ice forms preferentially.
Pooled water is one source, but the manual's named locations are shade, bridges and overpasses.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Patches of ice tend to develop in low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses.

questions.question: You must ride on a road covered with ice or snow. What does the manual advise?
choices: Keep the motorcycle straight up and proceed as slowly as possible
Lean the motorcycle slightly to load the tire edges
Maintain speed so the tires do not lose momentum
Use the rear brake continuously to keep the wheel loaded
questions.explanation: The manual says cautious riders avoid roads covered with ice or snow, and if you cannot, keep your motorcycle straight up and proceed as slowly as possible. If you must travel at a walking pace it suggests letting your feet skim the surface, keeping off the brakes, and squeezing the clutch lever to coast if possible.
choiceExplanations: Leaning uses traction for cornering that a slippery surface cannot supply.
Speed is the opposite of what the manual advises on ice.
The manual says to keep off the brakes if travelling at a walking pace, and to coast if possible.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Crash Avoidance and Hazards
source.sourceQuote: Patches of ice tend to develop in low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses.

questions.question: How should you normally cross railroad or trolley tracks that run across the road?
choices: Ride straight within your lane
Turn to take them at a 90 degree angle
Cross at 45 degrees
Stop, then walk the motorcycle across
questions.explanation: The manual says it is usually safer to ride straight within your lane to cross tracks, and warns that turning to take tracks at a 90 degree angle can be more dangerous, because the direction may put you into another lane of traffic.
choiceExplanations: Turning to square them up can put you into another lane of traffic, which is the greater danger.
Forty-five degrees is the rule for seams that run parallel to your path, not across it.
Nothing in the manual requires dismounting at a level crossing.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c

questions.question: Tracks or pavement seams run parallel to your path of travel. How do you cross them?
choices: Move far enough away to cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees, then make a deliberate turn
Ride straight within your lane, as you would for tracks that cross the road
Cross at the shallowest angle possible to avoid a jolt
Straddle the seam until it ends
questions.explanation: The manual gives a different rule for parallel hazards: for track and road seams that run parallel to your path, move far enough away from tracks, ruts, or pavement seams to cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees, then make a deliberate turn so you are not thrown off balance.
choiceExplanations: Riding straight along a parallel seam keeps your wheel in it, which is exactly the trap.
A shallow angle lets the seam capture the front wheel and steer it.
Straddling a seam keeps the hazard under the motorcycle instead of behind it.

questions.question: Which rule applies to a track crossing the road, and which to a seam running parallel to your path?
choices: Ride straight in your lane across a crossing track; cross a parallel seam at 45 degrees or more
Cross both at 90 degrees
Cross both at 45 degrees
Ride straight in your lane for both
questions.explanation: The two rules are deliberately different. For tracks crossing the road it is usually safer to ride straight within your lane. For tracks, ruts or pavement seams that run parallel to your path, move far enough away to cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees and make a deliberate turn.
choiceExplanations: Turning to 90 degrees at a level crossing can steer you into another lane.
Forty-five degrees applied to a track crossing the road means an unnecessary turn in traffic.
Riding straight along a parallel seam keeps the wheel in the groove.

questions.question: Riding over rain grooves or a bridge grating makes the motorcycle weave. What should you do?
choices: Relax, maintain a steady speed and ride straight across
Slow sharply until the weaving stops
Zigzag with the grooves to stay in your lane
Accelerate hard to ride over the top of the grooves
questions.explanation: The manual says the uneasy, wandering feeling caused by rain grooves and bridge gratings is generally not hazardous: relax, maintain a steady speed and ride straight across. Crossing at an angle forces riders to zigzag to stay in the lane, and the zigzag is far more hazardous than the wandering feeling.
choiceExplanations: Sharp slowing is a sudden input on a surface where sudden inputs are unhelpful.
The manual says the zigzag is far more hazardous than the wandering feeling.
Hard acceleration is not the manual's answer and adds an unnecessary input.

questions.question: What does the manual say about the weaving sensation on a bridge grating?
choices: It is generally not hazardous
It indicates a loose steering head bearing
It means the tires have lost traction
It is the first sign of a front tire going flat
questions.explanation: The manual reassures riders that the uneasy, wandering feeling produced by riding over rain grooves or bridge gratings is generally not hazardous. Knowing that is what allows you to hold a steady speed and ride straight across instead of correcting into a zigzag.
choiceExplanations: Steering problems are discussed under wobble, which is a different, speed-independent shake.
The surface is making the tires track the grooves, not making them slide.
Tire failure is signalled by a change in handling, not by the grating-induced weave.

questions.question: Why does the manual warn against sudden moves on a slippery surface?
choices: Any sudden change in speed or direction can cause a skid
Sudden moves make the motorcycle harder for drivers to see
Sudden moves use more fuel on a low-traction surface
Sudden moves cause the suspension to bottom out
questions.explanation: The manual's rule is 'avoid sudden moves' because any sudden change in speed or direction can cause a skid, and it tells you to be as smooth as possible if you have to speed up, shift gears, turn or brake. Smoothness is the technique that low traction demands.
choiceExplanations: Conspicuity is a separate topic; the concern here is traction.
Fuel use is never part of the manual's safety reasoning.
Suspension travel is not what the manual warns about on slippery surfaces.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
